title: Entropy-tail contraction as an early-warning signal for test-time adaptation collapse
one_line_idea: Monitor the lower tail of the prediction-entropy distribution during test-time adaptation and use its contraction as an automatic trigger for resets before accuracy silently collapses.
problem: Entropy-minimization test-time adaptation can collapse to trivial predictions on long streams, and practitioners only discover the collapse after the fact because no online signal flags it without labels.
core_hypothesis: Collapse is preceded by a detectable contraction of the low-entropy tail of the prediction-entropy distribution several hundred samples before accuracy visibly degrades, because the model first over-commits on easy samples before corrupting hard ones.
core_claim: A label-free monitor tracking rolling percentiles of prediction entropy can trigger resets that prevent most collapse episodes while rarely firing on healthy adaptation runs.
method_sketch: Instrument standard entropy-minimization adaptation with rolling estimates of low and mid entropy percentiles, define a contraction statistic relative to the run's own early window, trigger a partial reset of adapted parameters when the statistic crosses a threshold, and evaluate on corruption streams of varying length and severity.
falsifiable_prediction: On long corruption streams where vanilla entropy minimization collapses, the tail-contraction statistic will cross its threshold before the accuracy drop in the large majority of collapse episodes, and threshold-triggered resets will retain most of the peak adapted accuracy.
why_important: Silent collapse is the main practical objection to deploying test-time adaptation, and a cheap label-free early-warning signal would make long-horizon adaptation far safer.
why_possibly_novel: Collapse mitigation work mostly modifies the objective or adds regularizers, whereas an explicit online collapse predictor driving reset scheduling appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat collapse as a forecastable event with its own leading indicator rather than a failure to be regularized away.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run entropy-minimization adaptation on a handful of long synthetic corruption streams, log entropy percentiles and accuracy per window, and check whether tail contraction temporally precedes accuracy drops.
main_risk: The lead time between tail contraction and accuracy collapse may be too short or too variable across streams to act on.
kill_risk: If collapse episodes show no consistent preceding entropy-tail signature, the monitor has no signal to exploit and the idea dies.
community_default_belief: Collapse in test-time adaptation should be prevented by better objectives and regularization, not detected and managed as an operational event.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every proposed regularizer has failure regimes on some stream, so a detection-and-reset layer may be the more robust primitive because it does not depend on the specific failure mechanism.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: A single afternoon run logging entropy histograms alongside accuracy on one collapsing stream; if the histogram shows no structure before the drop, abandon.

title: Cumulative parameter-drift budgets for long-horizon test-time adaptation
one_line_idea: Replace per-step learning-rate tuning in test-time adaptation with an explicit budget on cumulative parameter distance from source weights, enforced by projection.
problem: Test-time adaptation methods control per-step update size but not total excursion from the source model, so long streams accumulate drift that eventually destroys source knowledge regardless of step size.
core_hypothesis: Long-horizon adaptation failure is governed primarily by cumulative parameter drift from the source solution rather than by instantaneous step size, so directly budgeting the drift radius stabilizes arbitrarily long streams.
core_claim: Projecting adapted weights back onto a fixed-radius ball around source weights whenever the budget is exceeded yields more stable long-stream accuracy than tuned learning-rate decay at matched short-stream performance.
method_sketch: Add a projection step after each adaptation update that rescales the weight delta to a maximum norm per layer group, sweep the radius on short validation streams, and compare against learning-rate schedules on streams an order of magnitude longer than those used for tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched accuracy on short streams, drift-budgeted adaptation will degrade substantially less than learning-rate-tuned adaptation as stream length grows, and the best radius will transfer across corruption types better than the best learning rate.
why_important: Stream length at deployment is unknown and unbounded, so a stability mechanism whose guarantee does not weaken with stream length addresses the core deployment risk of test-time adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: Trust-region-style constraints are common in reinforcement learning and fine-tuning, but an explicit cumulative-drift budget as the primary stability control for test-time adaptation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Stability should be parameterized by where the weights are allowed to go, not by how fast they move.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement norm-ball projection on top of one standard entropy-minimization method and compare long-stream accuracy curves against the same method with its best learning-rate schedule.
main_risk: A fixed radius may be too rigid, blocking genuinely needed adaptation under severe shifts while permitting harmful drift under mild ones.
kill_risk: If no radius simultaneously permits useful adaptation and prevents long-stream degradation, the single-budget framing is refuted.
community_default_belief: Careful learning-rate selection and episodic resets are the accepted tools for keeping test-time adaptation stable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learning-rate tuning controls a local quantity while the failure is global displacement, so the accepted tool addresses a proxy rather than the cause.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One long stream, one method, three radii versus three learning rates; if radius curves are not systematically flatter, drop the idea.

title: A phase diagram for statistics-only versus gradient-based test-time adaptation
one_line_idea: Map empirically when recalibrating normalization statistics alone beats gradient-based adaptation as a function of batch size and shift severity, yielding a practitioner decision rule.
problem: Practitioners must choose between cheap normalization-statistics recalibration and riskier gradient-based adaptation, but the literature offers point comparisons rather than a map of which regime favors which approach.
core_hypothesis: There exists a reproducible crossover surface in the batch-size by shift-severity plane below which statistics-only recalibration dominates gradient adaptation, and the surface position is predictable from a cheap unlabeled divergence estimate.
core_claim: A two-dimensional empirical phase diagram, built once on synthetic shift ladders, transfers well enough to natural shifts to serve as a method-selection rule without target labels.
method_sketch: Sweep batch size and corruption severity across several architectures, record which adaptation family wins in each cell, fit a boundary, then test whether the fitted boundary predicts the winning family on held-out natural shift datasets using estimated severity.
falsifiable_prediction: The winning-family boundary fitted on synthetic corruptions will predict the better method on the majority of held-out natural shift settings, substantially above a coin flip.
why_important: Method selection under shift is done by folklore today, and even a coarse validated decision rule would save large amounts of compute and prevent harmful adaptation choices.
why_possibly_novel: Individual comparisons exist, but a systematic phase-diagram treatment with a transferability test of the boundary itself appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Turn the methods debate into cartography with a falsifiable claim about boundary transfer.
minimal_falsification_experiment: A coarse four-by-four grid over batch size and severity with one backbone, checking whether a clean monotone boundary even exists before scaling up.
main_risk: The boundary may depend strongly on architecture and normalization type, fragmenting the diagram into cases too numerous to be useful.
kill_risk: If winning regions are interleaved with no coherent boundary, the phase-diagram framing itself is refuted.
community_default_belief: Gradient-based adaptation is generally worth its cost when shift is nontrivial, and statistics recalibration is a weak baseline.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The weak-baseline reputation may come from evaluations concentrated in large-batch severe-shift regimes, leaving the small-batch mild-shift regime where recalibration could dominate under-measured.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run both families at two batch sizes and two severities on one dataset; if the ranking never flips, the diagram is trivial and the idea is unnecessary.

title: Augmentation-agreement objectives to replace entropy in single-sample test-time adaptation
one_line_idea: Adapt on single test samples by maximizing prediction agreement across label-preserving augmentations instead of minimizing entropy, removing the confirmation-bias incentive of confidence maximization.
problem: Single-sample test-time adaptation with entropy minimization rewards the model for becoming confident about its current guess, which amplifies initial errors precisely when the model is wrong.
core_hypothesis: Cross-augmentation agreement is a less biased adaptation signal than entropy because it can be improved by moving toward representations invariant to nuisances without requiring increased confidence in any particular class.
core_claim: Replacing the entropy term with an augmentation-agreement term in otherwise identical single-sample adaptation reduces error amplification on initially misclassified samples while matching gains on correctly classified ones.
method_sketch: For each test sample, generate a small set of photometric and geometric augmentations, adapt normalization and affine parameters to minimize pairwise prediction divergence across the set, and stratify evaluation by whether the source model was initially correct on the sample.
falsifiable_prediction: On the initially wrong stratum, agreement-based adaptation will flip predictions toward correct substantially more often than entropy-based adaptation, which will predominantly reinforce the initial error.
why_important: Single-sample adaptation is the only feasible mode for many deployment settings, and its current failure mode on hard samples is exactly where help is most needed.
why_possibly_novel: Consistency losses are widespread in semi-supervised learning, but a stratified analysis positioning agreement as a debiased replacement for entropy in the single-sample regime appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Evaluate adaptation objectives by their effect conditioned on initial correctness, exposing confirmation bias directly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one corrupted validation set, run both objectives sample-wise and compare flip-to-correct versus flip-to-wrong rates stratified by initial correctness.
main_risk: Augmentation agreement may be maximizable by degenerate constant predictions, requiring an anti-collapse term that reintroduces the bias being removed.
kill_risk: If flip-to-correct rates do not improve on the initially wrong stratum, the debiasing story fails.
community_default_belief: Entropy minimization is an acceptable universal surrogate for test-time adaptation because confident predictions correlate with correct ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The correlation holds on-distribution but inverts on the samples that matter under shift, where the model is confidently wrong.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: A few hundred single-sample adaptation episodes with both objectives, requiring only hours on one GPU, comparing stratified flip rates.

title: Mid-uncertainty gating: adapt only on samples the model is neither sure nor hopeless about
one_line_idea: Gate test-time adaptation updates to samples in an intermediate uncertainty band, hypothesizing that confident samples contribute nothing and hopeless samples inject noise.
problem: Test-time adaptation updates on every sample, but updates from already-confident samples are redundant and updates from severely off-manifold samples push parameters in essentially random directions.
core_hypothesis: The useful learning signal in unsupervised adaptation is concentrated in an intermediate uncertainty band, and restricting updates to that band improves both stability and final accuracy at reduced compute.
core_claim: A simple two-threshold gate on prediction entropy retains the large majority of adaptation gains while cutting harmful updates enough to visibly flatten long-stream degradation.
method_sketch: Add lower and upper entropy thresholds to a standard adaptation method, updating only on samples in between, calibrate thresholds on a short stream prefix, and compare full-stream accuracy and update counts against ungated adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Gated adaptation will match or exceed ungated accuracy while performing far fewer updates, and ablating the upper threshold will hurt more on severe shifts while ablating the lower threshold will hurt more on mild shifts.
why_important: A gate that improves stability while cutting compute makes adaptation viable on edge devices where both stability and energy budgets are binding.
why_possibly_novel: Sample selection for adaptation exists in fragments, but the specific two-sided band hypothesis with its severity-dependent ablation signature appears untested (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Both tails of the uncertainty distribution are useless for adaptation, for opposite reasons.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One method, one stream, a coarse grid over the two thresholds, checking whether any band setting dominates ungated adaptation on accuracy and update count simultaneously.
main_risk: The informative band may shift over the stream as the model adapts, requiring online threshold tracking that complicates the story.
kill_risk: If no static or tracked band setting beats ungated adaptation, the concentration hypothesis is refuted.
community_default_belief: More unlabeled adaptation data is better, so methods should update on every available test sample.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under shift the per-sample update quality varies enormously, and averaging good and bad updates can be strictly worse than keeping only the good ones.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Rank one stream's samples by entropy offline, then re-run adaptation using only middle-band samples; a single run answers whether the band retains the gains.

title: Stochastic restart schedules for test-time adaptation inspired by restart heuristics in optimization
one_line_idea: Treat resets in continual test-time adaptation as a first-class scheduling problem and test whether stochastic restart schedules dominate both never-resetting and fixed-interval resetting on recurrent-shift streams.
problem: Resets are used ad hoc in continual adaptation, with fixed intervals or heuristic triggers, and there is no principled account of how restart timing should relate to the stream's shift dynamics.
core_hypothesis: For streams with recurring or piecewise-stationary domains, restart timing behaves like restart scheduling in stochastic optimization, where heavy-tailed random schedules are robust to unknown segment lengths and outperform any fixed interval chosen without knowledge of the stream.
core_claim: A heavy-tailed stochastic restart schedule achieves within a small margin of the best post-hoc fixed interval on every tested stream, whereas each fixed interval fails badly on streams mismatched to it.
method_sketch: Construct streams with controlled segment-length distributions, run continual adaptation under never-reset, several fixed intervals, and heavy-tailed random schedules, and compare regret against the per-stream best schedule chosen in hindsight.
falsifiable_prediction: The stochastic schedule's worst-case regret across stream families will be substantially lower than that of any single fixed interval, mirroring the robustness pattern known from restart heuristics in optimization.
why_important: Deployment streams have unknown and changing dynamics, so robustness to schedule mismatch matters more than peak performance under a known stream.
why_possibly_novel: The analogy between adaptation resets and optimization restart theory, tested with regret-style evaluation, appears unexplored in the adaptation literature (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Import restart-schedule robustness thinking from optimization into continual adaptation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three synthetic stream families with different segment statistics, five schedules, one backbone, comparing worst-case regret across families.
main_risk: Resets discard useful accumulated adaptation on slowly varying streams, and the stochastic schedule may pay too much on exactly those streams.
kill_risk: If a single fixed interval is near-optimal across all realistic stream families, schedule robustness is a non-problem and the idea is moot.
community_default_belief: Reset timing is a minor implementation detail dominated by the choice of adaptation objective.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On long heterogeneous streams the timing of forgetting may control more accuracy variance than the objective, since every objective eventually accumulates error without resets.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One recurrent-shift stream, compare never-reset, one fixed interval, and one heavy-tailed schedule; if all three tie, timing does not matter and the idea dies early.

title: Matching normalization-statistics forgetting rates to measured stream shift timescales
one_line_idea: Estimate the timescale of distribution drift online and set the momentum of running normalization statistics to match it, instead of using one fixed momentum for all streams.
problem: Adaptive normalization methods use a fixed exponential-moving-average momentum, implicitly assuming a single drift timescale, so they over-smooth fast-changing streams and over-react on slow ones.
core_hypothesis: A substantial fraction of the performance variance of normalization-based adaptation across streams is explained by the mismatch between the fixed momentum and the stream's actual drift timescale, which can be estimated online from feature-mean autocorrelation.
core_claim: An online controller that sets momentum from an estimated drift timescale recovers most of the gap to the per-stream oracle momentum without labels or tuning.
method_sketch: Estimate autocorrelation of batch feature means over a sliding window, map the estimated decorrelation time to a momentum value through a fixed rule, and evaluate against fixed-momentum baselines and per-stream oracle momentum on streams with different drift speeds.
falsifiable_prediction: Across streams spanning slow to fast drift, the controller will track the oracle momentum ranking, and the fixed-momentum baseline's shortfall will grow with the mismatch between its implied timescale and the stream's measured one.
why_important: Normalization recalibration is the cheapest and most deployed adaptation mechanism, so removing its hidden timescale assumption improves a very wide base of systems.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptive momentum has been touched on heuristically, but grounding the momentum choice in an explicit online drift-timescale estimate with an oracle-gap evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat the momentum hyperparameter as a measurable property of the stream, not a tuning knob.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize streams with known drift timescales, verify the autocorrelation estimator recovers them, then check whether momentum-matched runs beat fixed momenta.
main_risk: Feature-mean autocorrelation may confound class-composition changes with domain drift, mis-estimating the timescale on class-bursty streams.
kill_risk: If oracle momentum varies little across streams with very different drift speeds, the mismatch premise is wrong and the controller is pointless.
community_default_belief: A single well-chosen momentum works across deployments, and stream-specific tuning is unnecessary refinement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Published evaluations concentrate on streams with similar drift statistics, hiding the sensitivity that heterogeneous real streams would expose.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Sweep momentum on two streams with very different drift speeds; if the optimal momenta coincide, the premise fails immediately.

title: Label-prior-corrected entropy objectives to stop minority-class erasure in test-time adaptation
one_line_idea: Jointly estimate the target label marginal online and subtract its influence from the entropy-minimization objective so adaptation stops collapsing minority classes under label shift.
problem: Entropy minimization under label shift preferentially raises confidence on majority classes, progressively erasing minority-class predictions in a self-reinforcing loop that standard class-balancing heuristics only partially interrupt.
core_hypothesis: The minority-erasure loop is driven by the mismatch between the implicit uniform-prior assumption of entropy objectives and the true drifting target prior, and correcting the objective with an online prior estimate removes the loop at its source.
core_claim: Adaptation with an online prior-corrected objective preserves minority-class recall under simultaneous covariate and label shift where uncorrected and heuristically balanced variants degrade it substantially.
method_sketch: Maintain a running estimate of the target label marginal from calibrated predictions, reweight or re-center the adaptation loss by the estimated prior each window, and evaluate on streams with controlled joint covariate and prior drift, tracking per-class recall trajectories.
falsifiable_prediction: On streams with skewed drifting priors, minority-class recall under the corrected objective will remain within a small margin of its starting value while uncorrected entropy minimization shows monotone minority-recall decay.
why_important: Real deployment streams almost always combine covariate and label shift, and silent minority-class erasure is a serious failure that aggregate accuracy metrics hide.
why_possibly_novel: Label-shift estimation and test-time adaptation are mature separately, but closing the loop with an online prior estimate inside the adaptation objective, evaluated on per-class trajectories, appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Diagnose entropy collapse as a prior-mismatch problem rather than a regularization problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One stream with fixed covariate shift and a scripted prior drift, comparing per-class recall curves of corrected versus uncorrected objectives.
main_risk: Prior estimates from a model that is itself degrading may be biased in exactly the direction that reinforces rather than corrects the loop.
kill_risk: If per-class recall decay persists under oracle prior correction, the mismatch hypothesis is wrong and the mechanism dies.
community_default_belief: Class-balanced sampling or diversity regularizers adequately handle label imbalance during test-time adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Those heuristics treat symptoms at the batch level while the objective itself keeps pulling toward the majority prior on every update.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run adaptation with an oracle target prior plugged into the objective on one skewed stream; if minority recall still decays, abandon the framing.

title: Probe-routed layer selection: choose which layers to adapt from a cheap shift-type probe
one_line_idea: Use a lightweight probe that classifies the incoming shift as appearance-like or semantic-like from layer-wise feature divergences, then unfreeze only the layer range appropriate to that shift type.
problem: Test-time adaptation methods fix which parameters to adapt in advance, yet sensor-style shifts plausibly live in early layers and semantic shifts in later ones, so a fixed choice is wrong for a large fraction of streams.
core_hypothesis: Layer-wise divergence profiles between source statistics and incoming target features carry enough signal to route adaptation to the correct depth range, and depth-matched adaptation beats both all-layer and fixed-subset adaptation.
core_claim: A divergence-profile router adds negligible overhead and improves accuracy over the best fixed layer subset when evaluated across a pool of heterogeneous shift types, because no fixed subset is right for all of them.
method_sketch: Precompute per-layer source feature statistics, measure per-layer divergence on a small target buffer, classify the profile shape with a tiny rule or classifier, unfreeze the indicated depth range, and evaluate across shift types spanning corruptions, style changes, and class-composition changes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a heterogeneous shift pool, routed adaptation will beat every fixed layer subset in aggregate, while on any single homogeneous shift type the matched fixed subset will tie it, confirming the gain comes from routing rather than capacity.
why_important: A reliable router turns one adaptation system into a family of specialists, which matters wherever a single deployed model faces qualitatively different shifts over its lifetime.
why_possibly_novel: Layer-choice studies exist as static ablations, but closing the loop from an online shift-type probe to depth routing appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The first question adaptation should answer is where in the network the shift lives, not how strongly to adapt.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Verify on a small shift pool that divergence profiles cluster by shift family, then compare routed against fixed-subset adaptation on held-out shifts from each family.
main_risk: Profiles for mixed or compound shifts may be ambiguous, causing routing errors that are worse than a safe fixed default.
kill_risk: If divergence profiles do not separate shift families even on clean synthetic cases, routing has no input signal and the idea dies.
community_default_belief: Adapting normalization parameters everywhere is a safe universal choice, making layer selection an unnecessary complication.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniform adaptation spends its stability budget on layers that do not need to move, and this cost is invisible in short-stream benchmarks but plausibly dominant in long heterogeneous ones.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute layer-wise divergence profiles for two obviously different shift types on one backbone; if the profiles look identical, the routing signal does not exist.

title: Burstiness-controlled evaluation protocols that expose ordering sensitivity of test-time adaptation
one_line_idea: Introduce an evaluation protocol where the run-length distribution of classes and domains in the test stream is a controlled parameter, revealing how method rankings change with temporal correlation.
problem: Most test-time adaptation evaluations shuffle test data, but real streams are temporally correlated in both class and domain, and correlation strength is exactly the condition that breaks batch-statistics assumptions.
core_hypothesis: Rankings of adaptation methods are unstable across the burstiness axis, with methods relying on batch class-diversity degrading sharply as run lengths grow, so single-point shuffled evaluations systematically misrank methods for deployment.
core_claim: A protocol sweeping run-length distributions from shuffled to highly bursty produces method-ranking reversals on standard corruption benchmarks and provides a burstiness-robustness score that shuffled protocols cannot recover.
method_sketch: Generate stream orderings with parameterized run-length distributions over classes and domains from existing benchmark data, run a representative set of adaptation methods across the sweep, and report accuracy as a function of burstiness alongside ranking-stability statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: At least some pairs of methods that differ clearly under shuffled ordering will reverse order under high burstiness, and the reversal points will be consistent across datasets sharing the same backbone.
why_important: If rankings depend on an ordering parameter that benchmarks fix arbitrarily, the community may be optimizing methods for a regime deployments never see.
why_possibly_novel: Non-independent streams have been studied for specific methods, but burstiness as a swept first-class evaluation axis with ranking-stability analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Make temporal correlation a dial on the benchmark, not a footnote in the appendix.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reorder one corruption benchmark at three burstiness levels and evaluate three popular methods; ranking reversal at any level validates the concern.
main_risk: Reversals may occur only at burstiness levels beyond anything realistic, making the protocol technically correct but practically irrelevant.
kill_risk: If rankings are stable across the entire sweep, ordering sensitivity is a non-issue and the protocol adds nothing.
community_default_belief: Shuffled test streams are an acceptable simplification because ordering effects are second-order relative to shift severity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Batch-composition assumptions are load-bearing in many adaptation objectives, and ordering directly controls batch composition, making it plausibly first-order.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One method known to use batch statistics, one stream re-ordered by class into long runs; a sharp accuracy drop confirms ordering is first-order in an afternoon.

title: Domain-snapshot memory: cache and reuse adaptation states for recurring domains
one_line_idea: Fingerprint incoming stream segments with cheap feature statistics, cache adapted normalization and affine states per fingerprint, and reload cached states when a previously seen domain recurs.
problem: Continual adaptation treats every domain change as novel, re-paying the full adaptation cost and error even when the stream revisits domains it has already handled, as day-night or weather cycles do.
core_hypothesis: Recurrence is common enough in realistic streams that a small memory of per-domain adaptation states, keyed by unlabeled feature fingerprints, converts most domain re-entries into near-instant recoveries instead of fresh adaptation transients.
core_claim: Snapshot memory reduces cumulative regret on recurrent-shift streams relative to continual adaptation without memory, with the advantage growing in the number of revisits and never hurting on non-recurrent streams beyond a small routing overhead.
method_sketch: Compute rolling feature-moment fingerprints, match against a bounded library with a divergence threshold, load the matched snapshot or spawn a new slot on mismatch, update the active slot online, and evaluate on cyclic corruption schedules against memoryless baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: On streams that revisit each domain several times, per-revisit error transients will shrink to near zero for the memory system while remaining constant for memoryless adaptation, producing a cumulative accuracy gap that grows with cycle count.
why_important: Cyclic environmental change is the norm in outdoor and industrial deployments, so exploiting recurrence is a large free win that current formulations ignore.
why_possibly_novel: Episodic memory appears in continual learning with labels, but a label-free fingerprint-keyed state cache for test-time adaptation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat adaptation states as reusable assets indexed by where the stream has been before.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One cyclic stream alternating two corruptions, memory of size two, comparing transient error at each re-entry against a memoryless baseline.
main_risk: Fingerprint collisions between similar domains could load a wrong snapshot, and wrong-state loading may be worse than fresh adaptation.
kill_risk: If re-entry transients are already negligible for memoryless methods, the recurrence savings the memory targets do not exist.
community_default_belief: Continual test-time adaptation should adapt forward through whatever comes, with forgetting managed by regularization rather than by explicit reuse.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regularized forgetting still pays a re-learning transient at every revisit, and the total transient cost across cycles can dwarf what regularization saves.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure the re-entry transient of a strong continual method on a two-domain cyclic stream; if the transient is near zero, memory has nothing to save.

title: Per-sample state routing for streams that interleave multiple domains simultaneously
one_line_idea: Maintain several concurrent adaptation states and route each incoming sample to the state matching its inferred domain, addressing streams where multiple domains interleave sample by sample.
problem: Existing continual adaptation assumes one active domain at a time, but many real streams interleave sources, such as multi-camera feeds multiplexed into one model service, so a single adaptation state chases an unstable mixture.
core_hypothesis: When interleaving is present, a single global adaptation state converges to a compromise that is worse than the unadapted source model for at least some component domains, while per-sample routing to a small set of states recovers close to per-domain adapted accuracy.
core_claim: Lightweight per-sample domain inference from instance-level feature statistics is accurate enough to route updates and predictions, and routing dominates the single-state baseline as the interleaving factor grows.
method_sketch: Simulate interleaved streams by multiplexing distinct corruption domains at controlled mixing ratios, cluster instance-normalization statistics online to assign samples to states, adapt each state only on its assigned samples, and sweep the number of states and mixing ratio.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-state accuracy will decline monotonically with the interleaving factor and fall below the frozen source model for some mixtures, while routed accuracy will stay near the per-domain adapted ceiling until the state budget is exceeded.
why_important: Model-serving architectures increasingly multiplex heterogeneous clients through shared models, making the interleaved regime a common but unevaluated deployment reality.
why_possibly_novel: Mixture-of-experts ideas exist in training-time adaptation, but online per-sample state routing for test-time adaptation with an interleaving-factor analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Break the one-domain-at-a-time assumption baked into continual test-time adaptation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multiplex two corruption domains at even mixing, compare single-state adaptation, frozen source, and two-state oracle-routed adaptation to bound what routing could gain.
main_risk: Instance-level statistics may be too noisy for reliable routing at realistic batch sizes, collapsing the routed system toward the single-state behavior.
kill_risk: If single-state adaptation handles even strongly interleaved mixtures without falling below source accuracy, the failure the router fixes does not occur.
community_default_belief: Domain changes in streams are sequential, so continual adaptation along a timeline is the right abstraction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregation layers in real serving stacks destroy temporal contiguity, delivering precisely the interleaved regime the sequential abstraction excludes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One fifty-fifty interleaved stream and a single-state method; if accuracy stays above the frozen source model, the claimed failure mode needs rethinking.

title: Order-robustness certification: score adaptation methods by their spread over stream orderings
one_line_idea: Quantify each test-time adaptation method by the spread of its accuracy over many orderings of the same sample set, and report worst-ordering performance as a certification-style metric.
problem: Two methods with equal mean accuracy can differ enormously in how badly an unlucky or adversarial stream ordering can hurt them, and current evaluations never measure this spread.
core_hypothesis: Ordering-induced accuracy spread varies widely across current methods, is largely uncorrelated with mean accuracy, and near-worst-case orderings can be found cheaply with greedy search, making order-robustness a distinct measurable axis of method quality.
core_claim: A certification-style report combining mean accuracy with empirical worst-found-ordering accuracy changes which methods look preferable for safety-relevant deployments.
method_sketch: For a fixed sample set, evaluate each method over many random orderings plus greedy adversarial orderings constructed by sequentially picking the next sample that maximally degrades running accuracy, then report mean, spread, and worst-found values per method.
falsifiable_prediction: Methods will show materially different spreads at matched means, and greedy orderings will degrade some methods far below their random-ordering range while barely affecting others.
why_important: Deployments cannot choose their stream order, so a method that is excellent on average but fragile to ordering is unsuitable for safety-relevant use, and the field currently cannot tell such methods apart.
why_possibly_novel: Adversarial inputs are heavily studied, but adversarial and worst-case orderings of clean inputs as an evaluation primitive for adaptation appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The adversary controls only the order of the data, never the data itself.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take two popular methods and one corruption set, evaluate over a few dozen random orderings plus one greedy ordering each, and compare spreads at matched means.
main_risk: Greedy ordering search may find only mild degradations, understating true worst-case behavior and weakening the certification claim.
kill_risk: If spreads are tiny and near-identical across methods, ordering robustness is not a differentiating axis and the metric is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Averaging over a few random stream orders adequately characterizes an adaptation method's behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation dynamics are path-dependent by construction, and path-dependent systems generically exhibit heavy-tailed sensitivity to input ordering that means conceal.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Twenty random orderings of one stream for one stateful method; a wide accuracy histogram immediately proves the axis matters.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: Tiny fractions of delayed weak labels as an anchor for drifting test-time adaptation
one_line_idea: Study how small a fraction of delayed, possibly noisy labels suffices to anchor unsupervised test-time adaptation against drift, mapping the label-fraction versus stability trade-off curve.
problem: Purely unsupervised adaptation drifts on long streams, yet many deployments do eventually receive some labels through audits or user corrections, and no one has quantified how much anchoring such sparse delayed feedback provides.
core_hypothesis: The stabilizing value of labels under drift is strongly concave, so a very small fraction of delayed labels recovers most of the gap between unsupervised adaptation and a fully supervised oracle, primarily by correcting the estimated label prior and re-centering decision thresholds.
core_claim: Even labels delayed by thousands of samples and corrupted by moderate noise provide most of their anchoring value, because their role is drift correction rather than instance-level teaching.
method_sketch: Augment a standard adaptation method with a replay buffer of delayed labeled samples applied at their arrival time, sweep label fraction, delay, and label-noise level on long drifting streams, and plot final and time-averaged accuracy against each axis.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy as a function of label fraction will rise steeply and then plateau at a small fraction, and increasing delay will shift the curve only mildly until the delay approaches the stream's drift timescale.
why_important: The result would tell practitioners exactly how little labeling infrastructure suffices to make adaptation safe, converting an open-ended risk into a budgetable cost.
why_possibly_novel: Semi-supervised adaptation exists, but the systematic mapping of delay, noise, and fraction as a three-axis anchoring budget for streaming adaptation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Frame labels as drift anchors with a measurable exchange rate rather than as training data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One long drifting stream, three label fractions at fixed delay, comparing time-averaged accuracy to unsupervised and fully supervised references.
main_risk: Under severe concept drift the anchoring value of stale labels may collapse, making the concavity claim regime-dependent in ways that complicate the message.
kill_risk: If accuracy grows near-linearly with label fraction, the concavity story fails and sparse labeling offers no special leverage.
community_default_belief: Test-time adaptation research should assume zero labels because any labeling makes the problem ordinary semi-supervised learning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The zero-label idealization discards a resource almost every real deployment has in small quantities, and the interesting regime is exactly the sparse delayed one that neither literature covers.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Add one percent delayed labels to a drifting run and compare drift curves with and without; a visible flattening in one run justifies the full study.

title: Compute-gated adaptation: skip updates on easy samples and spend the budget where it matters
one_line_idea: Insert a cheap gate that predicts whether an adaptation update on the current batch is worth its compute, targeting a fixed update budget while retaining most of full adaptation's accuracy.
problem: Test-time adaptation multiplies inference cost by requiring backward passes on every batch, which is unaffordable on edge hardware, yet many batches plausibly contribute little to adaptation.
core_hypothesis: Adaptation progress per update is highly unequal across batches, and a gate using forward-pass statistics such as entropy change and feature-divergence spikes can identify the high-value updates in advance, so a small fraction of updates achieves most of the accuracy gain.
core_claim: At a fixed small update budget, gated adaptation retains the large majority of full adaptation's improvement over the frozen source model, while random update skipping at the same budget loses much more.
method_sketch: Define gate features from forward statistics, calibrate a threshold to hit a target update rate, run on standard corruption streams at several budgets, and compare gated, random-skip, and full adaptation on accuracy versus backward-pass count.
falsifiable_prediction: The accuracy-versus-updates curve for the gate will dominate random skipping at every budget, with the gap largest at small budgets, and gate decisions will correlate with retrospectively measured per-update accuracy gains.
why_important: Compute is the binding constraint for adaptation on embedded systems, and an order-of-magnitude reduction in backward passes at minor accuracy cost would move adaptation from research to practice in those settings.
why_possibly_novel: Efficient adaptation work focuses on parameter subsets, whereas value-of-update gating in the time dimension with budgeted evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ration adaptation over time by predicted marginal value, not just over parameters.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrospectively measure per-update accuracy gains along one adaptation run, verify inequality across updates, then test whether forward statistics predict the high-gain updates.
main_risk: Update value may be path-dependent, so skipping low-value updates changes the trajectory and invalidates the retrospective value estimates the gate learns from.
kill_risk: If per-update gains are near-uniform across batches, there is nothing for a gate to exploit and budgeted adaptation reduces to random skipping.
community_default_belief: Adaptation cost is treated as acceptable overhead, with efficiency addressed by adapting fewer parameters rather than fewer steps.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Parameter-subset methods still pay a backward pass per batch, so the time dimension holds the remaining order of magnitude that parameter methods cannot reach.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Log per-update accuracy deltas on one stream and plot their distribution; strong inequality across updates is visible in a single run and justifies building the gate.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: Jointly adapting the model and the abstention threshold under distribution shift
one_line_idea: Treat the abstention threshold as an adaptable parameter updated jointly with the model during test-time adaptation, rather than fixing it from source-domain calibration.
problem: Selective prediction systems fix their abstention threshold using source-domain confidence statistics, but adaptation changes the confidence distribution online, silently invalidating the threshold and the coverage-risk trade-off it was chosen for.
core_hypothesis: Under shift with adaptation, the confidence distribution moves enough that a fixed threshold badly misses its target coverage or risk, and an online threshold controller tracking a running confidence quantile restores the intended operating point at negligible cost.
core_claim: Joint model-and-threshold adaptation achieves a strictly better realized risk-coverage frontier on shifted streams than adapt-then-fixed-threshold, and the gap widens with shift severity and adaptation aggressiveness.
method_sketch: Wrap a standard adaptation method with a controller that re-solves for the threshold each window from running confidence quantiles targeting fixed coverage, evaluate realized risk and coverage over drifting streams, and compare against fixed thresholds calibrated on source data.
falsifiable_prediction: Fixed thresholds will show coverage drifting far from target as streams shift, while the controller holds coverage near target with lower realized risk at matched average coverage.
why_important: Abstention is the standard safety mechanism for deployed classifiers, and an invalidated threshold quietly converts a safe system into an overconfident one precisely when shift makes errors likely.
why_possibly_novel: Selective prediction and test-time adaptation are both mature, but their interaction, where adaptation itself moves the confidence distribution under the fixed threshold, appears underexamined (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Adaptation breaks the abstention contract, so the contract must adapt too.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one adaptation method on a shifting stream and plot realized coverage under a fixed threshold over time; drift away from target coverage establishes the problem in one run.
main_risk: Quantile tracking uses the model's own possibly miscalibrated confidences, so the controller may hold nominal coverage while realized risk still degrades.
kill_risk: If realized coverage under fixed thresholds stays near target across severe shifts, the invalidation problem is minor and the controller unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Calibration and thresholding are post-processing concerns separable from adaptation dynamics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation continually rewrites the confidence distribution the post-processing was fit to, making separability an artifact of static evaluation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One stream, one fixed threshold, plot coverage over time during adaptation; visible drift in an afternoon confirms the interaction is real.

title: Accuracy-slope extrapolation: predicting long-horizon adaptation behavior from medium windows
one_line_idea: Measure the within-run trend of proxy performance over medium-length windows and test whether this slope predicts long-horizon collapse better than absolute benchmark scores do.
problem: Benchmarks evaluate adaptation on streams far shorter than deployment lifetimes, and a method's score on a short stream may say little about whether it degrades, stabilizes, or collapses over runs orders of magnitude longer.
core_hypothesis: The temporal trend of label-free proxies, such as agreement with the frozen source model and entropy statistics, measured over a medium window, is a stronger predictor of long-horizon accuracy than the short-window accuracy itself.
core_claim: A slope-based stability score computed from the first segment of a run predicts end-of-long-run accuracy ranking across methods and streams better than initial-segment accuracy ranking does.
method_sketch: Run many method-stream pairs for very long horizons, record early-window proxy slopes and early accuracy, then compare their rank correlations with final accuracy, and package the best predictor as a cheap stability screening protocol.
falsifiable_prediction: Across method-stream pairs, proxy-slope ranking will correlate with long-run outcome ranking markedly better than early-accuracy ranking, and pairs with negative proxy slopes will contain nearly all eventual collapses.
why_important: If cheap early signals can screen out methods destined to collapse, the community can evaluate long-horizon safety without the compute of exhaustive long-run benchmarking.
why_possibly_novel: Long-horizon collapse is documented anecdotally, but a quantitative early-predictor study treating stability forecasting as the object of study appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Benchmark the derivative, not just the value.
minimal_falsification_experiment: A dozen method-stream pairs run long enough to observe divergent outcomes, checking whether early proxy slopes separate collapsing from stable runs.
main_risk: Collapse may be abrupt rather than gradual for some methods, leaving no early slope signature to detect.
kill_risk: If early slopes and long-run outcomes are essentially uncorrelated, stability is not forecastable this way and the protocol is worthless.
community_default_belief: Higher benchmark accuracy on standard-length streams indicates a better adaptation method, full stop.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Short-stream accuracy and long-horizon stability may be traded off against each other by aggressive adaptation, making the standard metric actively misleading about deployment behavior.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Extend two methods with similar benchmark scores to a ten-times-longer stream and compare outcomes; divergence in one afternoon run demonstrates the metric gap.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: A label-shift diagnostic that decides when marginal feature alignment should be disabled
one_line_idea: Estimate target label-marginal divergence without labels and use it to modulate or disable marginal feature alignment in unsupervised domain adaptation, since alignment is provably counterproductive under strong label shift.
problem: Marginal feature alignment, the workhorse of unsupervised domain adaptation, forcibly matches feature distributions even when class proportions differ across domains, in which case perfect alignment necessarily misclassifies the excess mass of shifted classes.
core_hypothesis: A cheap label-marginal divergence estimate computed from source-classifier outputs on target data predicts when alignment strength should be reduced, and a simple gating rule on that estimate outperforms both always-on and always-off alignment across a spectrum of label-shift severities.
core_claim: Most of the benefit of sophisticated reweighted-alignment methods on label-shifted pairs is recoverable by the far simpler strategy of estimating the prior divergence first and gating a standard aligner accordingly.
method_sketch: Construct adaptation pairs with controlled label-shift severity from existing datasets, estimate target priors via confusion-corrected prediction aggregation, gate the adversarial or discrepancy alignment weight by the estimated divergence, and compare against fixed-weight baselines and reweighting methods.
falsifiable_prediction: Adaptation accuracy of always-on alignment will decline with label-shift severity and cross below the no-alignment baseline at some severity, while the gated variant will track the upper envelope of both baselines across the whole severity range.
why_important: Practitioners apply alignment by default, and a validated one-number diagnostic that flags when the default actively hurts would prevent a common silent failure.
why_possibly_novel: The harm of alignment under label shift is known theoretically, but packaging an estimator-plus-gate as a practical decision rule with a severity-sweep validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ask whether to align at all before asking how to align better.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three label-shift severities on one dataset pair, alignment on versus off, verifying the crossover exists and the prior-divergence estimate orders the severities correctly.
main_risk: Prior estimation from a shifted source classifier may itself be biased under strong covariate shift, corrupting the gate exactly where the decision matters most.
kill_risk: If no crossover between alignment-on and alignment-off appears even under extreme label shift, the diagnostic protects against a failure that does not manifest in practice.
community_default_belief: Feature alignment is a broadly safe default for unsupervised domain adaptation, with label shift handled as a refinement via importance weighting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The safe-default belief comes from benchmarks with nearly matched class proportions, which quietly exclude the regime where the default fails.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One dataset pair with priors made artificially extreme by subsampling, alignment on versus off; a same-day result shows whether harmful alignment is real at scale.

title: Geometry-ranked pseudo-label curricula that bypass source-confidence bias
one_line_idea: Order target pseudo-labels for self-training by neighborhood agreement in feature space rather than by classifier confidence, decoupling curriculum order from the source model's shifted confidence estimates.
problem: Confidence-ranked self-training curricula inherit the source model's biases, admitting confidently wrong pseudo-labels early on shifted classes, and errors admitted early compound through the curriculum.
core_hypothesis: Local geometric consistency of target features, measured as label agreement among mutual nearest neighbors, ranks pseudo-label reliability better than source-classifier confidence under shift, because geometry reflects the target manifold while confidence reflects the source decision surface.
core_claim: Swapping the curriculum ranking signal from confidence to neighborhood agreement, holding everything else fixed, reduces accumulated pseudo-label error and improves final target accuracy on pairs with pronounced shift.
method_sketch: Extract target features from the current model, build a mutual nearest-neighbor graph, score each sample by neighbor pseudo-label agreement, admit samples into self-training in agreement order, and compare against the identical pipeline ranked by confidence across several adaptation pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: The precision of admitted pseudo-labels in early curriculum stages will be higher for geometry ranking than for confidence ranking, and the gap in final accuracy will correlate with the measured calibration error of the source model on the target domain.
why_important: Self-training remains the strongest practical adaptation recipe, and its dominant failure mode is early admission of confident errors, so a better admission signal upgrades a very widely used tool.
why_possibly_novel: Neighborhood consistency has been used as an auxiliary filter, but a controlled like-for-like comparison establishing geometry as the primary curriculum signal under shift appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Under shift, trust where a sample sits among its peers over what the classifier feels about it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one adaptation pair, compute both rankings and compare pseudo-label precision at equal admission budgets before running any training.
main_risk: Neighborhood agreement can be confidently wrong in coherent clusters of systematically mislabeled samples, admitting compact blocks of errors that confidence ranking would have spread out.
kill_risk: If admission-budget precision curves for the two rankings are indistinguishable across pairs, the geometric signal adds nothing and the idea dies before training.
community_default_belief: Classifier confidence, with thresholds and class balancing, is the natural and adequate ordering signal for pseudo-label curricula.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence is exactly the quantity distorted by domain shift, so building the curriculum on it means building on the least trustworthy output of the system.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Precision-at-budget curves for both rankings on one dataset pair, computable in hours from cached features without any adaptation runs.

title: Estimate class-space overlap first: a two-stage recipe for partial and open-set domain adaptation
one_line_idea: Replace end-to-end instance weighting in partial and open-set adaptation with an explicit first stage that estimates which classes are shared, followed by standard adaptation restricted to the estimated shared space.
problem: Partial and open-set adaptation methods fold the question of which classes exist in the target into instance-level weights learned jointly with alignment, entangling two problems so failures cannot be attributed and weights drift with training dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Class-space overlap is estimable from aggregate prediction statistics before any adaptation, and conditioning a standard closed-set adapter on the estimated overlap outperforms joint end-to-end weighting because it removes a moving target from the optimization.
core_claim: A decoupled estimate-then-adapt pipeline matches or beats joint partial-domain-adaptation methods while providing an interpretable intermediate artifact, the estimated shared-class set, whose errors explain most downstream failures.
method_sketch: Aggregate source-classifier outputs on target data into class-presence scores using prior-corrected counting, threshold to select the shared set, run a standard adapter with source data restricted to that set, and evaluate on partial-overlap benchmarks with varied hidden-class fractions.
falsifiable_prediction: Presence-score accuracy will be high on benchmark pairs, the two-stage pipeline will match joint methods when the estimate is correct, and pipeline failures will concentrate almost entirely on pairs where the presence estimate errs, demonstrating clean attribution.
why_important: Real deployments rarely share exactly the training label space, and a modular recipe whose failure is diagnosable at the estimation stage is far easier to trust and debug than entangled joint objectives.
why_possibly_novel: Class-presence estimation exists implicitly inside joint methods, but promoting it to an explicit validated first stage with attribution analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Make which classes are actually there a measured quantity, not a by-product of training.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On existing partial-adaptation splits, evaluate presence-score detection of the true shared set from frozen source predictions alone, before building the full pipeline.
main_risk: Under strong covariate shift the source classifier may systematically miss present classes whose appearance changed, biasing presence estimates in ways prior correction cannot fix.
kill_risk: If presence estimation is unreliable precisely on the benchmark pairs where joint methods succeed, decoupling loses to entanglement and the recipe is refuted.
community_default_belief: Joint end-to-end optimization of instance weights and alignment is the right way to handle label-space mismatch because the two problems inform each other.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The joint formulation lets alignment errors corrupt the weights and weight errors corrupt alignment, a feedback loop that decoupling breaks at the modest price of a one-shot estimate.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute class-presence scores from cached predictions on one partial-overlap pair and check against ground truth; a few hours of work reveals whether stage one is viable.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: Shift-descriptor-conditioned prediction of adaptation hyperparameters across dataset pairs
one_line_idea: Learn a mapping from cheap unlabeled shift descriptors of a source-target pair to good adaptation hyperparameters, so new pairs get tuned settings without target-label validation.
problem: Adaptation hyperparameters tuned on one source-target pair transfer poorly to others, and since target labels are unavailable by definition, per-pair tuning is impossible in the setting the methods claim to address.
core_hypothesis: Good hyperparameters are a systematic function of measurable pair properties, such as feature-divergence statistics, estimated prior divergence, and source-model confidence profiles, and this function can be fit on a corpus of pairs with known outcomes and applied to unseen pairs.
core_claim: A descriptor-conditioned hyperparameter predictor closes a substantial fraction of the gap between default settings and per-pair oracle tuning on held-out dataset pairs, without using any target labels at prediction time.
method_sketch: Assemble many source-target pairs from existing benchmark suites, run a grid of hyperparameters per pair to record oracle settings, extract unlabeled descriptors per pair, fit a regressor from descriptors to settings, and evaluate the regret of predicted settings on held-out pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: Predicted settings will achieve markedly lower regret against oracle than fixed defaults on held-out pairs, and ablating divergence descriptors will hurt prediction more than ablating dataset-size descriptors.
why_important: Hyperparameter fragility is a chief reason adaptation methods disappoint in practice, and a transferable predictor converts accumulated benchmark compute into practical tuning guidance for new problems.
why_possibly_novel: Meta-learning of optimizer settings exists, but a shift-descriptor-based hyperparameter predictor specifically for unsupervised adaptation, validated by held-out-pair regret, appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Spend benchmark compute once, then amortize tuning across every future domain pair.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ten pairs, one adaptation method, a small grid; check whether oracle settings correlate with any descriptor at all before fitting a predictor.
main_risk: Oracle hyperparameters may be dominated by idiosyncratic dataset properties invisible to unlabeled descriptors, leaving the predictor no better than defaults.
kill_risk: If oracle settings show no descriptor-explainable structure across pairs, the mapping does not exist and the approach is dead.
community_default_belief: Adaptation methods should be made hyperparameter-insensitive by design, since tuning without target labels is impossible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Insensitivity by design has repeatedly failed to materialize, while the impossibility argument overlooks that tuning experience from other pairs is transferable evidence.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Scatter-plot oracle learning rates against feature divergence over existing published-style grid runs on a handful of pairs; visible correlation in an afternoon justifies the corpus effort.

title: Depth-profiled alignment: align features only at layers where divergence actually lives
one_line_idea: Measure layer-wise source-target divergence first, then apply alignment losses only at the depths where divergence concentrates, instead of aligning at one conventional layer.
problem: Alignment losses are conventionally applied at the penultimate layer regardless of where in the network the domain difference actually resides, potentially distorting layers that were already aligned while missing the ones that diverge.
core_hypothesis: Divergence profiles across depth vary strongly by shift type, and matching the alignment depth to the measured profile improves adaptation over penultimate-only alignment, with the improvement proportional to how far the measured peak sits from the penultimate layer.
core_claim: A profile-matched aligner is a drop-in change to standard adaptation pipelines that yields consistent gains on shifts whose divergence peaks early, such as sensor and style shifts, while being neutral on semantically shifted pairs.
method_sketch: Compute per-layer distributional divergence between source and target activations with a consistent estimator, place alignment losses at the top-divergence layers with weights proportional to divergence, and compare against fixed-depth alignment across shift types with known character.
falsifiable_prediction: Gains over penultimate-only alignment will correlate across pairs with the distance between the measured divergence peak and the penultimate layer, approaching zero when the peak is already there.
why_important: A free diagnostic that tells practitioners where to align makes a ubiquitous technique more reliable without new objectives or architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-layer alignment exists with uniform or heuristic weights, but driving depth selection from a measured divergence profile with a correlation-based validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Alignment should follow a measurement, not a convention.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Profile three shift types on one backbone, confirm the peaks differ by shift type, then compare profile-matched against penultimate alignment on the pair with the earliest peak.
main_risk: Activation divergence estimators may be unreliable in high dimensions at feasible sample sizes, making profiles noisy enough to misplace the alignment depth.
kill_risk: If divergence profiles are flat or identical across shift types, depth selection has no signal to work from.
community_default_belief: Penultimate-layer alignment is adequate because deep representations funnel all relevant domain differences to the top of the network.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The funnel intuition ignores that normalization layers can absorb or relocate divergence at every depth, leaving the true mismatch wherever normalization failed to absorb it, not necessarily at the top.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One backbone, two shift types, per-layer divergence curves from cached activations; distinct peak locations in a day of work validate the premise.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: A contagion model of pseudo-label error propagation in iterative self-training
one_line_idea: Model the spread of pseudo-label errors through rounds of self-training as a contagion process on the feature-space neighborhood graph, yielding a predicted divergence threshold from measurable initial conditions.
problem: Iterative self-training sometimes converges to strong target accuracy and sometimes degenerates, and there is no quantitative account predicting which outcome will occur from initial error rate and data geometry.
core_hypothesis: Error propagation is governed by a reproduction-number-like quantity, the expected number of new errors induced per existing error per round, computable from initial error rate, class confusability, and neighborhood-graph connectivity, with degeneration occurring when it exceeds one.
core_claim: A contagion model calibrated on synthetic adaptation problems predicts the convergence-versus-degeneration outcome of self-training on real adaptation pairs from measurements available before the first training round.
method_sketch: Formalize per-round error induction on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph, estimate the model's parameters from the source model's initial predictions and target feature geometry, predict outcomes for many adaptation pairs, then run full self-training to verify the predictions.
falsifiable_prediction: The estimated reproduction number will separate degenerating from converging runs with high accuracy across pairs, and interventions that lower it, such as stricter admission thresholds, will move outcomes across the predicted boundary.
why_important: Self-training is the backbone of modern adaptation, and a predictive theory of its failure would replace trial-and-error with a measurable go or no-go criterion.
why_possibly_novel: Error accumulation is discussed qualitatively, but a calibrated epidemic-style quantitative model with pre-run outcome prediction appears unexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Give self-training collapse a basic reproduction number.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On synthetic two-domain Gaussian problems where every quantity is controllable, verify the predicted threshold separates converging from degenerating self-training runs.
main_risk: Real error propagation depends on representation drift during training, which a static-graph contagion model may capture too crudely for quantitative prediction.
kill_risk: If outcomes on synthetic problems do not track the predicted threshold even qualitatively, the contagion abstraction is wrong and the model dies at stage one.
community_default_belief: Whether self-training helps or collapses is an empirical matter settled per dataset by trying it with standard safeguards.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The empirical-only stance may persist simply because no one has seriously attempted a quantitative propagation model, not because the dynamics are truly unpredictable.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulate label propagation with tunable initial error on one cached feature graph and check for a sharp threshold; a day of compute reveals whether threshold behavior exists at all.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: Bidirectional adaptation asymmetry as a label-free predictor of adaptation failure
one_line_idea: Run adaptation in both directions between source and target and use the asymmetry between the two runs' internal statistics as an unsupervised warning signal for unreliable adaptation.
problem: Practitioners have no label-free way to know whether an unsupervised adaptation run on a new pair succeeded or silently failed, since all observable losses can look healthy while target accuracy is poor.
core_hypothesis: Pairs where adaptation genuinely succeeds exhibit approximately symmetric behavior when the roles of source and target are swapped, whereas pathological pairs show large asymmetries in convergence speed, pseudo-label agreement, and final feature-divergence, making asymmetry a failure signal.
core_claim: An asymmetry score aggregated from bidirectional run statistics correlates strongly with true target accuracy across many adaptation pairs, enabling label-free triage of adaptation outcomes at the cost of one extra run.
method_sketch: For each pair, run the same adaptation method in both directions, extract paired trajectory statistics, define an asymmetry score, and correlate it with ground-truth target accuracy across a large corpus of pairs spanning benchmark suites.
falsifiable_prediction: The asymmetry score will rank pairs by adaptation reliability substantially better than one-directional internal metrics such as final alignment loss or mean confidence.
why_important: A trustworthy label-free success signal is arguably the biggest missing piece for deploying unsupervised adaptation, since without it every run requires labeled validation that the setting forbids.
why_possibly_novel: Reverse validation ideas exist for model selection, but a systematic study of directional asymmetry as a reliability signal across pairs appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: If adaptation only works one way round, it probably did not work at all.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ten pairs with known target accuracy, bidirectional runs, and a rank correlation between the asymmetry score and true accuracy.
main_risk: Genuine task asymmetries, such as one domain being intrinsically harder, may dominate the score and mask the failure signal it is meant to carry.
kill_risk: If asymmetry and true accuracy are uncorrelated across the corpus, the signal does not exist and the method is dead.
community_default_belief: Internal training metrics of a single adaptation run, such as alignment loss and pseudo-label confidence, are the available and adequate signals of adaptation health.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Those metrics are the very quantities the optimizer is paid to make look good, so they are systematically uninformative about failures the optimizer hides.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Bidirectional runs on three pairs chosen to span known-easy to known-hard; visible score separation in two days of compute justifies the full corpus study.

territory: Domain shift: domain adaptation/generalization, test-time adaptation, distribution-shift robustness, cross-site/cross-sensor transfer; academic ML only
title: Decomposing unsupervised adaptation gains into reweighting-equivalent and representation-change components
one_line_idea: Ablate adaptation methods against a matched importance-weighted classifier retrained on frozen source features to measure how much of their gain is achievable by reweighting alone.
problem: Reported gains of representation-learning adaptation methods are never decomposed, so the community cannot tell how much comes from genuinely new representations versus effects reproducible by cheap density reweighting on frozen features.
core_hypothesis: A meaningful fraction of headline adaptation gains on standard benchmarks is reweighting-equivalent, and the representation-specific residual varies sharply by shift type, being small for prior-dominated shifts and large for appearance shifts.
core_claim: A standardized two-component decomposition, computed by comparing each method against an importance-weighted frozen-feature baseline on the same pair, reveals systematic differences in where methods get their gains and identifies methods whose entire gain is reweighting-equivalent.
method_sketch: For each method and pair, train the frozen-feature reweighted baseline using density-ratio estimates, compute the gain split relative to the unadapted baseline and the full method, and tabulate the decomposition across methods, pairs, and shift types.
falsifiable_prediction: At least some published-style methods will show most of their gain matched by the reweighted baseline on prior-dominated pairs, while appearance-shift pairs will show large representation-specific residuals for the same methods.
why_important: The decomposition redirects research effort toward shifts where representation learning genuinely matters and exposes when expensive methods are re-deriving cheap statistical corrections.
why_possibly_novel: Reweighting and representation adaptation are compared as competitors, but using one as a decomposition baseline to attribute the other's gains appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Audit what adaptation methods actually buy beyond what a weighted classifier on frozen features already gets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One popular method, three pairs of differing shift character, the reweighted frozen-feature baseline, and the resulting gain split.
main_risk: Density-ratio estimation quality on high-dimensional features may cap the reweighted baseline artificially, inflating the apparent representation-specific component.
kill_risk: If the reweighted baseline is uniformly negligible across all pairs, the decomposition is degenerate and uninteresting.
community_default_belief: Gains of deep adaptation methods reflect learned domain-invariant representations, which is why they beat classical reweighting approaches.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep pipelines can implement implicit reweighting through sampling and loss dynamics, so their gains may partially be classical statistics wearing a representation-learning costume.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One pair, cached source features, one afternoon to train the importance-weighted classifier and compare its gain against a published-style method's reported margin reproduced locally.
