title: Re-auditing current-generation domain generalization against exhaustively tuned augmentation-heavy ERM
one_line_idea: Test whether the newest wave of domain generalization methods still beats empirical risk minimization once augmentation strength and model selection are equalized under a matched tuning budget.
problem: Earlier audits found that fair tuning erased most domain generalization gains over plain empirical risk minimization, but a new generation of methods has since appeared and has not been subjected to the same budget-matched discipline.
core_hypothesis: A substantial portion of currently reported gains of recent domain generalization methods over empirical risk minimization again disappears under equalized augmentation policies, equalized model-selection criteria, and matched tuning budgets.
core_claim: Budget-matched re-evaluation changes the apparent ranking of recent methods and shrinks the median reported gain over tuned empirical risk minimization substantially, identifying which method families retain real signal.
method_sketch: Select a representative set of recent methods, define a shared tuning protocol with identical augmentation search spaces and selection criteria, rerun all methods and the baseline under the shared protocol on standard multi-domain suites, and compare shrinkage of gains method by method.
falsifiable_prediction: The distribution of gains over the tuned baseline will contract toward zero relative to originally reported margins, with contraction largest for methods whose original evaluations used weaker baselines or asymmetric augmentation.
why_important: If the field's progress metric inflates under unequal tuning, resources flow to method families that do not actually help, and a periodic budget-matched audit is the community's error-correction mechanism.
why_possibly_novel: The audit methodology is established, but its application to the current method generation, with per-method shrinkage attribution, is new work that nobody has published for this cohort (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Audits depreciate; rerun the audit on the methods that postdate it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three recent methods and the tuned baseline on one multi-domain suite under the shared protocol, checking whether reported margins survive.
main_risk: Compute costs of honest matched tuning are large, and partial budgets could produce an audit vulnerable to the same criticism it makes.
kill_risk: If recent methods retain their full margins under matched budgets, the suspicion is wrong and the contribution reduces to a confirmation.
community_default_belief: Recent domain generalization methods represent genuine algorithmic progress over empirical risk minimization, as their published comparisons show.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The selection pressures that produced inflated margins in the previous generation, asymmetric tuning and favorable model selection, have not disappeared and plausibly operate on the current generation too.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Take one recent method's public configuration and re-tune only the baseline's augmentation with the same budget on one suite; margin collapse in that single comparison signals the broader audit is needed.

title: Does source-domain flatness actually predict the domain transfer gap once accuracy is controlled
one_line_idea: Run a large controlled correlation study testing whether sharpness measures computed on source domains predict out-of-domain accuracy drop after controlling for in-domain accuracy and model scale.
problem: Flat-minima arguments are widely invoked to justify weight averaging and sharpness-aware training for domain generalization, but the evidential basis is a handful of correlations that may be confounded by in-domain accuracy and architecture choices.
core_hypothesis: After controlling for in-domain accuracy, architecture, and training length, the partial correlation between standard sharpness measures and the domain transfer gap is much weaker than commonly assumed, and vanishes entirely for some shift types.
core_claim: A systematic partial-correlation analysis across hundreds of training runs shows that flatness is at best a shift-type-dependent predictor of transfer, contradicting its use as a general explanatory mechanism for domain generalization.
method_sketch: Train a large grid of models varying seeds, augmentation, optimizers, and flatness-inducing interventions on multi-domain datasets, measure several sharpness metrics on source data, and fit regressions predicting the transfer gap with and without controls.
falsifiable_prediction: Raw correlations between flatness and transfer will be visible but partial correlations under controls will shrink toward zero on at least some shift families, while interventions that change flatness without changing in-domain accuracy will move transfer inconsistently.
why_important: If flatness is not the operative mechanism, method development guided by it is optimizing a proxy, and identifying where the proxy fails redirects theory and practice.
why_possibly_novel: Individual papers report supporting correlations, but an adversarially controlled study designed to break the correlation, rather than confirm it, appears missing (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat the flatness-transfer link as a hypothesis to attack, not a lemma to assume.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fifty runs on one multi-domain dataset with matched in-domain accuracy pairs differing in sharpness, comparing their transfer gaps directly.
main_risk: Sharpness metrics disagree with each other, so a null result could be attributed to metric choice rather than to the absence of a real relationship.
kill_risk: If flatness robustly predicts transfer under all controls and metrics, the skeptical premise is refuted, though the confirmation would itself be a useful result.
community_default_belief: Flatter source minima transfer better across domains, which is why weight averaging and sharpness-aware methods help domain generalization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flatness-inducing interventions co-vary with implicit augmentation and ensembling effects, and the transfer benefit may come entirely from those covariates rather than from the geometry itself.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Construct a few matched-accuracy pairs differing in measured sharpness via optimizer settings on one dataset and compare transfer gaps; overlapping gaps in a week of small-scale runs would already undermine the strong claim.

title: Inferring latent training environments from per-sample gradient statistics for invariance penalties
one_line_idea: Cluster training samples by their gradient interactions with the model to recover latent environment structure, then apply environment-based invariance penalties without any environment labels.
problem: Invariance-based domain generalization methods require environment labels that most real datasets lack, and existing label-free partitioning heuristics rely on a trained reference model's errors, capturing only one axis of latent structure.
core_hypothesis: Per-sample gradient vectors during training contain recoverable signatures of latent environment membership beyond what error-based splitting captures, and invariance penalties applied over gradient-inferred partitions recover a substantial share of oracle-environment gains.
core_claim: Gradient-signature clustering produces partitions that align better with hidden ground-truth environments than error-based splitting, and downstream invariance training on those partitions closes part of the gap to oracle environment labels.
method_sketch: On datasets with hidden environment annotations, compute low-dimensional projections of per-sample gradients at several checkpoints, cluster them, measure partition alignment with hidden environments, then train invariance-penalized models over inferred partitions and compare against error-splitting and oracle baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Partition-environment alignment will exceed error-based splitting on most datasets, and downstream worst-environment accuracy will order as oracle above gradient-inferred above error-split above unpartitioned training.
why_important: Removing the environment-label requirement is the difference between invariance methods being a benchmark exercise and being applicable to the vast majority of real datasets.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient features are used for data valuation and cleaning, but as an environment-discovery signal feeding invariance penalties they appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Environments leave fingerprints in how samples pull on the weights, not just in whether the model errs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with known hidden environments, gradient clustering at one checkpoint, and a direct alignment comparison against error-based splitting before any downstream training.
main_risk: Gradient signatures may primarily encode class and difficulty rather than environment, yielding partitions that reproduce label structure instead of domain structure.
kill_risk: If gradient partitions align with hidden environments no better than random or class-based partitions, the discovery signal is absent.
community_default_belief: Without environment labels, splitting by a reference model's errors is the available and essentially sufficient approach to latent-environment discovery.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Error-based splitting captures only samples the reference model already fails on, missing environment structure among correctly classified samples where gradients still differ.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Cache per-sample gradient projections on one annotated dataset and compute clustering alignment metrics in a day, before committing to any invariance training.

title: Predictive-feature redundancy as a trainable safeguard against unknown domain shift
one_line_idea: Regularize models to spread predictive weight across multiple decorrelated feature groups so that failure of any single feature family under shift leaves the prediction intact, and test redundancy as an out-of-domain robustness predictor.
problem: Models concentrate predictive weight on the few most efficient features, so a shift that damages exactly those features causes disproportionate failure even when other valid predictive signals remain in the input.
core_hypothesis: A redundancy objective that enforces several decorrelated feature subsets to each be independently predictive yields models whose worst-case accuracy over feature-ablation directions is higher, and this redundancy score predicts out-of-domain accuracy better than in-domain accuracy does.
core_claim: Redundancy-regularized training improves accuracy under natural shifts that damage dominant features, at modest in-domain cost, and the measured redundancy of any trained model predicts its shift robustness across a model zoo.
method_sketch: Partition penultimate features into groups, add losses making each group independently predictive while decorrelating groups, evaluate on shift benchmarks, and separately compute redundancy scores for diverse pretrained models to correlate with their published-style robustness measured locally.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a model zoo, the redundancy score will correlate with out-of-domain accuracy after controlling for in-domain accuracy, and redundancy-trained models will show smaller worst-direction drops under targeted feature corruption.
why_important: A robustness mechanism that requires no knowledge of the coming shift addresses the realistic setting where shift type is unknown at training time.
why_possibly_novel: Ensemble diversity and feature decorrelation are classic, but redundancy as an explicit single-model training target and as a measurable robustness predictor under natural shift appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Engineer graceful degradation into the feature space itself, the way redundant systems are engineered elsewhere.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without redundancy losses on one dataset and compare accuracy under corruptions chosen to disable texture-like versus shape-like cues.
main_risk: Enforced redundancy may simply duplicate the same underlying features in disguised form, adding cost without independent failure modes.
kill_risk: If redundancy scores do not predict robustness across the zoo after controls, the core measurement claim collapses.
community_default_belief: Out-of-domain robustness is best pursued through data diversity and scale rather than through architectural or objective-level redundancy engineering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Data scale mitigates shifts represented in the data, while engineered redundancy targets the orthogonal failure mode of over-reliance on any single feature family, which scale alone does not remove.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure feature-group ablation sensitivity for one standard model and one diverse-ensemble distillate on a shift set in two days; if concentrated and spread models degrade identically, the mechanism is not operative.

title: Shift-axis-targeted augmentation search from measured inter-domain differences
one_line_idea: Estimate the dominant axes of variation between available training domains and synthesize an augmentation policy concentrated along those axes, instead of applying generic heavy augmentation.
problem: Augmentation is the strongest practical tool for domain generalization, but policies are chosen generically, spending capacity on variations irrelevant to the deployment shift while under-covering the variation directions the domains actually exhibit.
core_hypothesis: The inter-domain differences measurable within the training set predict the character of future unseen-domain differences well enough that augmentation concentrated on the measured axes outperforms generic policies of equal strength on held-out domains.
core_claim: A pipeline that fits interpretable transformation directions between training domains, then samples augmentations extrapolating along them, beats matched-budget generic augmentation on leave-one-domain-out evaluation.
method_sketch: Fit parametric photometric and spatial transforms best mapping each domain toward each other domain, extract principal transformation directions, define an augmentation distribution extrapolating beyond observed magnitudes along them, and run leave-one-domain-out comparisons at matched augmentation budget.
falsifiable_prediction: Targeted augmentation will beat generic policies most on suites where the held-out domain continues the measured variation axes, and will lose its edge on suites where the held-out domain varies along genuinely novel axes.
why_important: Augmentation budget is finite, and pointing it at measured rather than imagined variation could extract more generalization from the same data and compute.
why_possibly_novel: Learned augmentation policies optimize in-domain validation accuracy, whereas deriving the augmentation space itself from measured inter-domain transformation directions appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let the training domains tell you which augmentations matter before you extrapolate.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-domain suite, fit photometric transform directions between two training domains and test whether extrapolated augmentation improves accuracy on the third, held-out domain.
main_risk: Unseen domains may vary along axes orthogonal to those measured, in which case targeting is no better and possibly narrower than generic coverage.
kill_risk: If targeted policies lose to generic ones even on suites with visibly continued variation axes, the extrapolation premise fails.
community_default_belief: Broad generic augmentation is the safest choice because one cannot know the direction of future shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Future shift direction is partially knowable from the structure of already-collected domains, and ignoring that information wastes the strongest available prior.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: A single leave-one-domain-out comparison with a hand-fit color-and-blur transform axis versus the same budget of generic augmentation, achievable in days on one suite.

title: Interpolation versus extrapolation decomposition of domain generalization benchmark scores
one_line_idea: Score each test sample of domain generalization benchmarks by whether it lies within the span of training domains in representation space, then report method performance separately on interpolation-like and extrapolation-like subsets.
problem: Benchmark scores average over test samples that range from near-duplicates of training-domain variation to genuinely novel variation, hiding whether methods improve true extrapolation or merely cover interpolation better.
core_hypothesis: Most reported domain generalization improvements concentrate on interpolation-like test samples, with method rankings on the extrapolation-like subset being flatter and sometimes reversed, revealing that the field is largely improving interpolation coverage.
core_claim: A sample-level interpolation score, computed from distances to the convex region spanned by training-domain features in a fixed reference embedding, cleanly decomposes benchmark performance and materially changes conclusions about which methods generalize.
method_sketch: Embed all samples with a fixed reference encoder, define an interpolation score per test sample from its position relative to training-domain feature hulls, split test sets by score, and re-tabulate published-style method comparisons on both subsets across standard suites.
falsifiable_prediction: Method-over-baseline gains on the interpolation subset will exceed gains on the extrapolation subset systematically across suites, and some method orderings will invert on the extrapolation subset.
why_important: If claimed generalization progress is mostly interpolation, the community is misreading its own progress, and future benchmarks should report the decomposition by default.
why_possibly_novel: Hull-based extrapolation analyses exist in learning theory, but a practical sample-level decomposition applied as an audit across domain generalization benchmarks appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Split every benchmark score into the part that required generalization and the part that did not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One suite, one reference encoder, the interpolation score, and a re-tabulation of two methods against their baseline on the two subsets.
main_risk: The decomposition depends on the reference embedding, and different encoders may split samples differently enough to muddy conclusions.
kill_risk: If gains are uniform across the interpolation spectrum for all methods, the decomposition reveals nothing and the audit is empty.
community_default_belief: Held-out-domain accuracy measures genuine out-of-distribution generalization, since the domain was never seen in training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unseen domains often lie within the variation span of seen domains in representation space, so held-out status does not imply extrapolation demand.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute interpolation scores for one benchmark's held-out domain in a day of embedding work; if a large fraction of test samples land inside training hulls, the concern is immediately substantiated.

title: Basin-controlled comparison of weight averaging versus explicit ensembling for domain generalization
one_line_idea: Test the hypothesis that weight averaging matches ensembling for domain generalization only when member models share a loss basin, by constructing matched member sets within and across basins.
problem: Weight averaging is widely adopted as a cheap replacement for ensembling in domain generalization, but the conditions under which averaging preserves ensemble robustness gains are asserted rather than mapped.
core_hypothesis: The robustness gain of weight averaging tracks the ensemble gain closely for basin-sharing members and collapses for members separated by loss barriers, making linear-mode connectivity a measurable precondition for averaging-based generalization methods.
core_claim: A controlled study varying member diversity from same-basin fine-tunes to independently trained runs shows averaging-versus-ensembling parity is predicted by measured barrier height, giving practitioners a cheap test for when averaging is safe.
method_sketch: Generate member sets at graded diversity levels, measure pairwise loss barriers along linear paths, evaluate averaged and ensembled variants on shift benchmarks, and regress the parity gap on barrier statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: The out-of-domain accuracy difference between ensembling and averaging will grow monotonically with measured barrier height, remaining near zero below a threshold and widening sharply above it.
why_important: Averaging-based recipes are replacing ensembles at scale for cost reasons, and knowing exactly when the substitution loses robustness prevents silent regressions in deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: Mode connectivity and weight averaging are both studied, but a barrier-controlled parity analysis specifically targeting out-of-domain robustness appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Make the folk precondition for weight averaging an actual measured variable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three member pairs spanning low, medium, and high measured barriers, comparing averaged versus ensembled shift accuracy for each pair.
main_risk: Barrier height and member functional diversity are confounded, so parity differences may track diversity benefits of ensembles rather than averaging failures.
kill_risk: If parity holds even across high-barrier members, the precondition story is wrong and averaging is more robust than the hypothesis allows.
community_default_belief: Weight averaging captures essentially the same generalization benefit as ensembling at a fraction of the inference cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The equivalence evidence comes mostly from fine-tuning regimes that guarantee shared basins, and the belief may quietly fail as practitioners average increasingly diverse checkpoints.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Average two independently trained models versus ensembling them on one shift benchmark; a large gap in one day of evaluation confirms the precondition matters.

title: Class-frequency structure of the domain gap and class-conditional generalization objectives
one_line_idea: Measure whether rare classes suffer disproportionately larger accuracy drops under domain shift and design objectives that specifically protect tail-class transfer.
problem: Domain generalization is evaluated with class-averaged metrics, but if the transfer gap concentrates in tail classes, the averaged view hides the failure that matters and misguides objective design.
core_hypothesis: Per-class transfer gaps anti-correlate with training class frequency because rare classes are represented by fewer, less diverse exemplars whose features entangle domain and class cues, so tail classes bear a disproportionate share of the domain gap.
core_claim: A frequency-stratified analysis across standard suites reveals a systematic tail-transfer penalty, and a class-conditional objective that upweights domain-diversity pressure on rare classes narrows it without hurting head classes.
method_sketch: Tabulate per-class in-domain versus out-of-domain accuracy across multi-domain suites and models, regress the gap on class frequency, then train with class-conditional invariance or augmentation weighting inversely tied to frequency and re-measure the stratified gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: The frequency-gap regression will show a significant negative slope across most suites, and the conditional objective will flatten the slope while leaving mean accuracy within noise of the baseline.
why_important: Tail classes are often the operationally critical ones, and a hidden tail-transfer penalty means deployed models are least reliable exactly where labels were scarcest.
why_possibly_novel: Long-tail learning and domain generalization are mature separately, but the interaction, the frequency structure of the domain gap itself, appears rarely measured or targeted (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ask who pays the domain gap, not just how large it is.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Per-class gap tabulation on one suite with one strong baseline model, testing for the negative frequency slope before any method work.
main_risk: Class frequency correlates with intrinsic difficulty and annotation quality, and disentangling these confounds from the frequency effect may require careful matched analyses.
kill_risk: If per-class gaps show no frequency structure, the premise is empty and the conditional objective has no target.
community_default_belief: Domain shift hurts classes roughly uniformly, so class-averaged metrics adequately summarize generalization performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniformity is assumed rather than checked, and the data-diversity mechanism gives a concrete reason to expect systematic non-uniformity aligned with frequency.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One afternoon of stratified evaluation using publicly available pretrained multi-domain checkpoints to plot per-class gap against frequency.

title: Pretraining-proximity stratification to deconfound domain generalization evaluations
one_line_idea: Quantify each benchmark test domain's proximity to a model's pretraining distribution and re-evaluate domain generalization methods stratified by that proximity, separating method gains from pretraining familiarity.
problem: Modern domain generalization pipelines start from large pretrained backbones, so a test domain that is out-of-distribution for the benchmark's training split may be well represented in pretraining data, confounding what generalization scores measure.
core_hypothesis: A meaningful share of measured benchmark performance is explained by pretraining-proximity of test domains rather than by the generalization method, and method rankings compress or change on low-proximity strata.
core_claim: A proximity score computed from pretraining-representative data statistics stratifies benchmark domains such that method gains shrink on the least familiar stratum, revealing how much of reported progress rides on pretraining coverage.
method_sketch: Approximate pretraining proximity via retrieval density in a pretraining-representative corpus or embedding-space likelihood proxies, score all test domains of standard suites, stratify existing method comparisons by proximity, and re-tabulate gains within strata.
falsifiable_prediction: Absolute accuracy will track proximity strongly, and method-over-baseline margins will be systematically smaller on the lowest-proximity stratum across suites and backbones.
why_important: If generalization scores partly measure pretraining familiarity, the community's conclusions about which methods generalize are entangled with an unreported variable that stratification can expose.
why_possibly_novel: Pretraining contamination is discussed for language evaluation, but systematic proximity stratification of vision domain generalization benchmarks appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Report every generalization score alongside how familiar the test domain already was to the backbone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score the domains of one suite with a retrieval-density proxy and check whether per-domain baseline accuracy tracks the score before stratifying any method comparisons.
main_risk: Proximity proxies computed without access to the true pretraining corpus may be too crude, and conclusions would inherit the proxy's biases.
kill_risk: If baseline accuracy is uncorrelated with every reasonable proximity proxy, the confound is negligible and stratification adds nothing.
community_default_belief: Held-out benchmark domains constitute out-of-distribution tests regardless of what the backbone saw during pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web-scale pretraining plausibly covers most benchmark domain styles, making many held-out domains in-distribution for the backbone even though the benchmark labels them novel.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Retrieval-density scores for a handful of benchmark domains against a public web-scale image index, correlated with known per-domain difficulty, achievable in days.

title: Shipping per-class feature moments instead of source data for source-free adaptation
one_line_idea: Distill the source dataset into compact per-class feature statistics released with the model, and test how much of the gap between source-free and source-present adaptation these statistics recover.
problem: Source-free adaptation discards all source information except the weights for privacy and logistics reasons, but the binary choice between full data access and none ignores intermediate artifacts that may be nearly as useful and far less sensitive.
core_hypothesis: Low-order per-class feature statistics of the source domain, orders of magnitude smaller than the data and arguably less privacy-sensitive, suffice to anchor target adaptation almost as well as source data access, because their main role is preventing class-semantics drift.
core_claim: Adaptation regularized toward shipped per-class feature moments recovers most of the accuracy difference between source-free and source-present adaptation across standard pairs, while the artifact size stays negligible relative to the model.
method_sketch: Precompute class-conditional feature means and covariance sketches on source data, add a drift penalty tying adapted target features to the shipped statistics, evaluate against source-free and source-present baselines, and ablate statistic order and size.
falsifiable_prediction: The moments-anchored method will land much closer to the source-present ceiling than to the source-free baseline on most pairs, with diminishing returns beyond second-order statistics.
why_important: A standardized small statistics artifact could become common release practice, improving downstream adaptation across the ecosystem without the privacy and bandwidth costs of data sharing.
why_possibly_novel: Feature-statistics regularizers appear inside individual methods, but framing the shipped artifact itself as a release-time design question with a size-utility curve appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Define the minimal source artifact worth shipping alongside weights for future adaptation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One adaptation pair, three conditions, source-free, moments-anchored, and source-present, comparing final target accuracy.
main_risk: Per-class statistics may leak more membership information than assumed, undermining the privacy argument that motivates the artifact.
kill_risk: If moments-anchoring recovers little of the source-present gap, the artifact is not worth standardizing and the framing collapses.
community_default_belief: Source-free adaptation should assume weights only, since any source artifact reintroduces the privacy and logistics problems the setting exists to avoid.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The all-or-nothing framing was never derived from actual privacy requirements, and low-order aggregate statistics plausibly sit on the acceptable side of most real constraints.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Add a class-mean anchoring penalty to one source-free method on one pair; a same-week accuracy jump toward the source-present ceiling validates the direction.

title: Composable low-rank domain deltas for sequential adaptation without forgetting
one_line_idea: Store each encountered domain's adaptation as a low-rank weight delta and handle new or recurring conditions by composing stored deltas, replacing destructive sequential fine-tuning.
problem: Sequential adaptation across a lifetime of domains overwrites earlier adaptations, and full per-domain checkpoints are too expensive, leaving no practical middle ground for models that must revisit and combine conditions.
core_hypothesis: Domain adaptations live approximately in low-rank subspaces that interfere weakly across domains, so arithmetic composition of per-domain deltas approximates jointly adapted models, including for compound conditions formed by combining previously seen factors.
core_claim: A delta library with lightweight composition weights matches sequential fine-tuning on each single domain while avoiding forgetting entirely, and outperforms both on compound domains composed of seen factors.
method_sketch: Adapt low-rank adapters per domain from a frozen base, store deltas, infer composition weights for incoming data from fingerprint similarity to stored domains, and evaluate on domain sequences with revisits and factor-combination test conditions.
falsifiable_prediction: On sequences with revisits, the library approach will show zero measured forgetting while sequential fine-tuning degrades earlier domains, and on compound conditions delta mixtures will beat both the base model and any single stored delta.
why_important: Deployed systems face recurring and combinable conditions, and a storage-efficient compositional memory turns lifelong adaptation from a stability problem into a retrieval problem.
why_possibly_novel: Task-vector arithmetic is studied for skills and fine-tuning tasks, but its systematic use for domain-shift libraries with fingerprint-driven composition on streams appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Treat domains as vectors and compound weather as vector addition.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two single-factor corruption domains and their combination, testing whether the summed deltas beat individual deltas and the base model on the compound condition.
main_risk: Delta interference may grow with library size, degrading composition quality exactly when the library becomes useful.
kill_risk: If summed deltas fail to help on even simple two-factor compounds, the compositionality premise is dead.
community_default_belief: Continual adaptation should update one set of weights forward in time, with forgetting controlled by regularization or replay.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The single-trajectory framing forces an unnecessary trade-off, since parameter-efficient deltas make storing and recombining the past cheap enough to sidestep forgetting altogether.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train two corruption adapters and evaluate their sum on the compound corruption in a day; compositional benefit or its absence is immediately visible.

title: Fast-slow twin divergence as an unsupervised stopping criterion for source-free adaptation
one_line_idea: Run two copies of the adapting model at different learning rates and stop adaptation when their prediction agreement starts falling, using twin divergence as a label-free overfitting alarm.
problem: Source-free adaptation lacks any validation signal, so practitioners cannot tell when continued adaptation stops helping and starts destroying the model, and fixed step counts are wrong for most pairs.
core_hypothesis: While adaptation extracts genuine target structure, differently paced copies converge toward similar predictions, but once the objective begins fitting noise the copies diverge, so the agreement trajectory between a fast and a slow twin peaks near the accuracy peak.
core_claim: Stopping at maximum twin agreement lands within a small margin of oracle-stopped accuracy across adaptation pairs and methods, at the cost of one extra model copy during adaptation only.
method_sketch: Duplicate the adapting model with a scaled learning rate, track windowed prediction agreement on incoming target data, stop both when agreement peaks, and compare stopped accuracy against oracle stopping and fixed-budget baselines across pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: The agreement peak will precede or coincide with the accuracy peak on most pairs, and agreement-stopped accuracy will dominate every fixed step budget evaluated across the same pairs.
why_important: A reliable label-free stopping rule removes one of the most consequential silent hyperparameters in source-free adaptation and makes unattended deployment plausible.
why_possibly_novel: Disagreement-based validation exists for model selection, but a paced-twin construction generating an online stopping signal during adaptation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Overfitting to a bad unsupervised objective announces itself as divergence between differently paced learners.

title: Mapping the interaction between self-supervised objective choice and shift type in source-free adaptation
one_line_idea: Systematically cross auxiliary self-supervised objectives with shift families to test whether the best adaptation objective is shift-type-dependent, producing a selection map instead of a universal recommendation.
problem: Source-free methods attach one self-supervised auxiliary task, chosen by author preference, yet different objectives plausibly repair different damage, and the field lacks any systematic objective-by-shift interaction study.
core_hypothesis: There is a strong interaction effect, with reconstruction-style objectives best under low-level sensor corruption, contrastive instance objectives best under style shift, and masked-prediction objectives best under occlusion-like shift, so no single auxiliary objective dominates.
core_claim: A full factorial study across objectives and shift families yields a reliable selection map, and choosing the objective per measured shift character beats the best fixed objective across a heterogeneous shift pool.
method_sketch: Fix the adaptation skeleton and swap only the auxiliary objective across reconstruction, contrastive, and masked-prediction families, evaluate on shift families with controlled character, test interaction significance, and validate map-based selection on held-out shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: The objective-by-shift interaction term will explain more outcome variance than the objective main effect, and map-based selection will beat the single best objective on the pooled evaluation.
why_important: The result converts an arbitrary design choice into a measurable decision, and a validated map benefits every source-free pipeline immediately.
why_possibly_novel: Individual objectives are compared incidentally in method papers, but a designed factorial with interaction analysis and a validated selection rule appears missing (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Stop asking which auxiliary task is best and start asking best for which shift.
minimal_falsification_experiment: A two-by-two of reconstruction versus contrastive objectives on corruption versus style shift, testing for the crossover the full map presupposes.
main_risk: Interactions may be dominated by dataset idiosyncrasies rather than shift character, making the map unstable across datasets.
kill_risk: If one objective dominates all shift families, the interaction premise is wrong and the map degenerates to a single recommendation.
community_default_belief: A well-chosen contrastive or clustering auxiliary objective is broadly sufficient for source-free adaptation across shift types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sufficiency claims come from evaluations concentrated on style-like academic benchmarks, leaving sensor-corruption and occlusion regimes where other objectives should win largely untested.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Swap reconstruction for contrastive in one public source-free pipeline on one corruption pair; a ranking flip against the style-pair result demonstrates the interaction in days.

title: Open-set stress testing of source-free adaptation objectives that inflate confidence on unknown classes
one_line_idea: Audit whether source-free adaptation objectives, which reward confident clustered predictions, systematically raise confidence on classes absent from the source label space, and design an objective term that prevents it.
problem: Source-free objectives reward confident, well-clustered target predictions, but when the target stream contains classes the source model never learned, the same pressure plausibly forces unknown-class samples into known classes with growing confidence.
core_hypothesis: Standard source-free adaptation measurably increases confidence on unknown-class samples relative to the unadapted model, degrading downstream open-set detection precisely because the objective cannot distinguish unknown-class clusters from known-class ones.
core_claim: An open-set stress protocol quantifies this confidence inflation across popular methods, and adding an unknown-mass reservation term, which permits a fraction of target data to remain unassigned, removes most of the inflation at minor cost to closed-set gains.
method_sketch: Inject disjoint-class samples into adaptation streams at controlled ratios, track unknown-sample confidence and open-set detection metrics before and after adaptation across methods, then evaluate the reservation term under the same protocol.
falsifiable_prediction: All tested confidence-maximizing methods will inflate unknown-class confidence relative to the frozen source model, with inflation growing in the unknown ratio, and the reservation term will cut inflation substantially while retaining most closed-set improvement.
why_important: Adaptation that silently destroys a model's ability to say none of the above converts a safety feature into a hazard, and no current benchmark measures this side effect.
why_possibly_novel: Open-set recognition and source-free adaptation are established separately, but auditing adaptation itself as a cause of open-set degradation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Adaptation objectives may be quietly training models to hallucinate familiarity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One method, one pair, unknown classes injected at one ratio, comparing unknown-sample confidence distributions before and after adaptation.
main_risk: The reservation term introduces a fraction hyperparameter whose miscalibration could either readmit the inflation or discard genuine known-class data.
kill_risk: If unknown-class confidence does not inflate under standard methods, the audited failure does not exist and both the protocol and fix are unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Source-free adaptation affects the known-class decision surface and is neutral with respect to open-set behavior, which is treated as a separate problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Entropy and clustering pressures act on all samples in the stream indiscriminately, and unknown-class samples are in the stream, so neutrality would be a coincidence rather than a property.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Adapt once with unknown injection and plot the unknown-sample confidence histogram shift in an afternoon; visible inflation settles the premise.

title: Buffer-free continual adaptation via generative replay of feature statistics rather than samples
one_line_idea: Prevent forgetting in continual test-time adaptation by replaying synthetic feature vectors drawn from stored per-domain statistical sketches instead of storing raw samples.
problem: Replay buffers stabilize continual adaptation but storing raw target samples is often prohibited by privacy or memory constraints, while regularization-only alternatives underperform on long heterogeneous streams.
core_hypothesis: For adaptation-scale updates, which mostly adjust normalization and light adapter parameters, replaying feature-level samples drawn from compact Gaussian-mixture sketches of past domains preserves stability nearly as well as raw-sample replay at a small fraction of the memory and none of the raw-data retention.
core_claim: Statistical-sketch replay matches raw replay within a small accuracy margin on continual adaptation benchmarks while storing only distribution parameters, making it deployable where raw retention is forbidden.
method_sketch: Maintain per-domain mixture sketches of intermediate features, sample synthetic features during adaptation updates to anchor past-domain behavior through partial forward passes, and compare against raw replay, regularization-only, and no-protection baselines on long multi-domain streams.
falsifiable_prediction: Sketch replay will recover most of the forgetting reduction of raw replay across streams, and its advantage over regularization-only baselines will grow with the number of distinct domains in the stream.
why_important: Privacy constraints are a hard blocker for raw replay in medical and consumer deployments, so a statistics-only substitute unlocks continual adaptation exactly where it is currently disallowed.
why_possibly_novel: Generative and feature replay exist in supervised continual learning, but distribution-sketch replay tailored to the lightweight parameter scope of test-time adaptation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Replay the distribution, not the data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: A two-domain sequential stream comparing forgetting under raw replay, sketch replay, and no replay with one adaptation method.
main_risk: Feature sketches may fail to capture the aspects of past domains that matter for stability, especially higher-order structure lost by mixture approximations.
kill_risk: If sketch replay performs no better than regularization-only baselines, the synthetic anchoring adds nothing and the approach dies.
community_default_belief: Effective replay requires stored real examples, and privacy-constrained systems must therefore settle for weaker regularization-based stability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The parameters adapted at test time are few and statistically coupled to low-order feature structure, which is exactly what compact sketches can preserve, so raw fidelity may be unnecessary at this update scale.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One sequential two-corruption run with class-conditional Gaussian sketch replay in place of a raw buffer; parity or failure is visible within a day.

title: Adaptation-trajectory descriptors as transferable warm starts for related shifts
one_line_idea: Record compact descriptors of completed adaptation trajectories and reuse them to warm-start adaptation on related shifts, testing whether adaptation experience itself transfers.
problem: Every adaptation run starts from scratch even when the organization has adapted the same base model to dozens of related shifts before, discarding accumulated procedural knowledge about how adaptation unfolds.
core_hypothesis: Adaptation trajectories for related shifts share structure, such as which parameter groups move and in what order, and initializing a new run from a trajectory-derived prior, rather than from the source model alone, reduces the samples needed to reach a given accuracy.
core_claim: A trajectory library indexed by shift fingerprints supports warm starts that reach target accuracy with substantially fewer target samples than cold starts, with the benefit predictable from fingerprint similarity between old and new shifts.
method_sketch: Log parameter-delta trajectories across many adaptation runs on a shift corpus, compress them into per-shift descriptors, warm-start new runs by applying a similarity-weighted initial delta, and measure sample-efficiency curves against cold starts as a function of fingerprint similarity.
falsifiable_prediction: Warm-started runs on shifts similar to library entries will show clear sample-efficiency gains, the gains will decay smoothly with fingerprint distance, and dissimilar warm starts will not hurt beyond a small margin.
why_important: Sample efficiency is the binding constraint for adaptation on short streams, and reusing procedural experience is a free resource every long-lived deployment accumulates.
why_possibly_novel: Meta-learning studies initialization for supervised tasks, but mining completed unsupervised-adaptation trajectories as reusable priors for future shifts appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Adaptation runs are data too; learn from how the model moved last time.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Adapt to one corruption, save the final delta, warm-start adaptation to a related corruption from a scaled version of it, and compare sample-efficiency curves against a cold start.
main_risk: Trajectory structure may be dominated by optimizer noise rather than shift identity, making descriptors uninformative and warm starts arbitrary.
kill_risk: If warm starts from highly similar shifts show no sample-efficiency gain, procedural transfer does not exist at this granularity.
community_default_belief: Each adaptation problem is self-contained, and the source model is the right initialization for every new target domain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Organizations face families of related shifts, not isolated ones, and the source-initialization convention ignores the strong prior that yesterday's related adaptation provides.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One warm-start-versus-cold-start comparison between two severities of the same corruption, runnable in a day, establishes whether any procedural transfer signal exists.

title: Cross-site collaboration through exchanged confusion structure instead of features or gradients
one_line_idea: Let multiple sites adapting the same base model exchange only their calibrated class-confusion structure, testing whether this minimal artifact improves each site's local adaptation.
problem: Sites facing related domain shifts could help each other adapt, but exchanging features or gradients raises privacy and bandwidth barriers, so in practice every site adapts alone.
core_hypothesis: The class-confusion structure a site develops under its shift, a tiny class-by-class matrix, carries transferable information about which class boundaries the shift family degrades, and priors built from other sites' confusion matrices improve local pseudo-label filtering and threshold setting.
core_claim: Confusion-structure exchange yields consistent adaptation improvements over isolated adaptation across simulated multi-site settings, at negligible communication cost and with far weaker privacy exposure than feature sharing.
method_sketch: Simulate sites as distinct shifted versions of shared benchmarks, estimate each site's confusion matrix via calibrated aggregation without labels or with small audit sets, share matrices across sites, incorporate them as pseudo-label admission priors, and compare against isolated adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Sites will show improved pseudo-label precision on the class pairs flagged as confusable by peer sites, with overall accuracy gains growing in the similarity of the sites' shifts.
why_important: A collaboration primitive compatible with strict privacy constraints could unlock network effects in adaptation for hospital consortia and sensor networks that currently cannot share anything.
why_possibly_novel: Federated learning exchanges gradients or weights, while adaptation literature ignores inter-site artifacts entirely; confusion-structure exchange as the minimal collaborative unit appears unexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Share which mistakes the shift causes, not the data that caused them.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two simulated sites with related corruptions, one-way confusion transfer, measuring pseudo-label precision improvement on flagged class pairs.
main_risk: Confusion structure may be too site-specific, so priors imported from peers misdirect filtering on class pairs that differ locally.
kill_risk: If imported confusion priors never improve pseudo-label precision even between sites with near-identical shifts, the transferable signal is absent.
community_default_belief: Meaningful multi-site collaboration for adaptation requires sharing representations, models, or gradients, as in federated learning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Much of adaptation's difficulty concentrates in a few shift-degraded class boundaries, and identifying those boundaries is cheap to communicate even though fixing them is expensive to learn.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute confusion matrices for two shifted variants of one dataset and check their agreement; high overlap in a day of work indicates transferable structure worth building on.

title: Adapter-twin disagreement as a cheap replacement for independently trained models in accuracy estimation
one_line_idea: Replace the independently trained model pairs used in disagreement-based accuracy estimation with parameter-efficient adapter variants of one base model, testing whether cheap twins preserve the accuracy-tracking property under shift.
problem: Disagreement between independently trained models tracks accuracy under shift, but training multiple full models is too expensive for practitioners who most need label-free accuracy estimates on large backbones.
core_hypothesis: Diversity injected through differently seeded lightweight adapters and augmentation streams on a shared frozen backbone produces disagreement statistics that track target accuracy nearly as well as full independent training, because the relevant diversity lives in the task head's view of the features rather than in the backbone.
core_claim: Adapter-twin disagreement estimates accuracy under a broad range of natural and synthetic shifts with error close to full-retraining disagreement at a small fraction of the training cost.
method_sketch: Train several adapter variants per backbone with varied seeds and augmentation, measure pairwise disagreement on shifted test sets with known accuracy, and compare estimation error against full independently trained pairs across shift benchmarks and backbone families.
falsifiable_prediction: The disagreement-accuracy relationship for adapter twins will remain tight across shift types, degrading only under shifts that specifically attack the shared frozen backbone's features, which the study will identify as the method's stated boundary.
why_important: Label-free accuracy estimation is the practical core of shift monitoring, and cutting its cost by an order of magnitude determines whether anyone actually deploys it.
why_possibly_novel: Disagreement-based estimation is established, but the systematic study of how little training independence suffices, using parameter-efficient twins, appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Find the minimum viable independence for disagreement-based monitoring.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One backbone, five adapter twins, one full-retraining pair, comparing disagreement-accuracy fits across one synthetic and one natural shift suite.
main_risk: Shared-backbone failure modes will be invisible to adapter disagreement, and such shifts may be more common in practice than the benchmark suite reveals.
kill_risk: If adapter-twin disagreement decouples from accuracy on most natural shifts, cheap twins are insufficient and the full cost is unavoidable.
community_default_belief: Disagreement methods require genuinely independent training runs, since shared components correlate errors and break the estimator.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The error correlation that matters is on shifted inputs near the decision boundary, and head-level diversity may decorrelate exactly those errors even with a shared backbone.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Five adapter twins on one shifted set with known accuracy, plotting disagreement against error in a day, immediately shows whether the cheap signal tracks.

title: Transferable shift-severity scores trained on synthetic corruption ladders
one_line_idea: Train a regressor that maps unlabeled batch statistics to a calibrated shift-severity scalar using synthetic corruption ladders, then test whether the score transfers to natural and cross-site shifts.
problem: Monitoring systems need a graded severity signal rather than a binary shift alarm, but existing detectors output uncalibrated statistics whose scale varies by dataset, model, and shift type.
core_hypothesis: Corruption ladders provide enough supervised structure, since severity levels are known by construction, to learn a severity mapping from model-internal statistics that generalizes zero-shot to natural shifts, because internal statistics respond to accuracy-relevant degradation in a shift-agnostic way.
core_claim: A ladder-trained severity regressor produces scores that rank natural shift conditions in agreement with their true accuracy impact, providing a calibrated monitoring signal with no target labels.
method_sketch: Generate corruption ladders across types, extract feature and confidence statistics per batch, train a regressor from statistics to severity level, and evaluate rank agreement between predicted severity and measured accuracy drop on held-out natural shifts and cross-site datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: Predicted severity will correlate strongly with actual accuracy drop on natural shifts never seen in training, and will outperform single-statistic baselines such as mean confidence or feature distance used alone.
why_important: A transferable severity dial enables graded operational responses, such as increasing abstention or triggering adaptation, instead of the all-or-nothing alarms current detectors support.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks are used for evaluation, but exploiting their built-in severity labels as supervision for a transferable monitoring signal appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Synthetic corruption ladders are free training data for shift measurement, not just an evaluation suite.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the regressor on half the corruption types, test severity ranking on the held-out types, and only then proceed to natural shifts.
main_risk: Severity may not be a one-dimensional quantity across shift families, so a scalar score could conflate mild accuracy-destroying shifts with severe benign ones.
kill_risk: If ladder-trained scores fail to rank even held-out corruption types, cross-family transfer is hopeless and the idea dies at stage one.
community_default_belief: Shift detection is a two-sample testing problem, and severity beyond detection is not something unlabeled statistics can calibrate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two-sample framing discards the ordinal supervision that synthetic ladders provide for free, which may be exactly enough to calibrate a useful accuracy-relevant scale.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One backbone, ladders from a standard corruption suite, a linear regressor on confidence and feature statistics, and held-out-type ranking checked within days.

title: Layer-wise divergence fingerprints for automated shift-type diagnosis
one_line_idea: Classify the type of an incoming distribution shift, sensor-level, style-level, semantic, or prior, from the profile of feature divergences across network depth, enabling automated choice of mitigation.
problem: Different shift types demand different responses, recalibration, adaptation, retraining, or prior correction, but monitoring systems detect that a shift happened without characterizing what kind it is.
core_hypothesis: Shift families leave distinguishable signatures in the depth profile of source-target feature divergence, with sensor shifts peaking early, style shifts mid-network, semantic shifts late, and prior shifts appearing predominantly in output statistics rather than features.
core_claim: A fingerprint classifier trained on constructed shifts of known type assigns correct types to held-out shifts, including natural ones, accurately enough to route mitigation choices better than any fixed policy.
method_sketch: Construct labeled shift instances of each family from existing datasets, compute depth-divergence profiles plus output-statistics features, train a small classifier, validate on held-out natural shifts with human-adjudicated type labels, and evaluate routed mitigation against fixed responses.
falsifiable_prediction: Fingerprint classification will exceed chance by a wide margin on held-out shift families, and mitigation routed by predicted type will outperform the best single mitigation across a mixed pool of shift events.
why_important: Automated diagnosis is the missing middle layer between shift detection and shift response, and getting it right turns monitoring from alerts into actions.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-localization of shift has been observed qualitatively, but a validated shift-type taxonomy with a trained fingerprint classifier and downstream routing appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Move from detecting distribution shift to diagnosing its species.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Profiles for three constructed shift types on one backbone, checking linear separability of the profiles before training anything.
main_risk: Natural shifts are mixtures of types, and mixture profiles may not decompose into recognizable pure-type components.
kill_risk: If pure-type profiles already overlap heavily on constructed cases, the fingerprint signal is too weak to support diagnosis.
community_default_belief: Shift response selection is a human expert judgment, since automated systems can at best detect that something changed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The expert's own diagnosis draws on signals like which processing stages look wrong, and depth-divergence profiles plausibly capture the same evidence in measurable form.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two-type profile separability on cached activations from one model, computable in a day, decides whether the diagnostic signal exists.

title: Prediction-graph structure as an early detector of harmful shift
one_line_idea: Monitor the consistency between feature-space neighborhood structure and predicted labels on incoming data, and use breakdowns of this structure as a label-free signal of accuracy-destroying shift.
problem: Input-distribution detectors alarm on any change, including harmless ones, while the quantity that matters, whether accuracy silently dropped, is unobservable without labels, so monitoring systems drown in false alarms.
core_hypothesis: When shift harms accuracy, predicted labels become inconsistent with feature-space neighborhood structure, with neighbors increasingly receiving different labels, and this structural inconsistency rises before or with accuracy loss while remaining flat under benign shift.
core_claim: A neighborhood label-agreement statistic on incoming batches separates harmful from benign shifts substantially better than input-statistics detectors, reducing false alarms at matched detection rates for true accuracy drops.
method_sketch: Build streaming nearest-neighbor structure over recent feature vectors, compute per-window agreement between neighbor predictions, calibrate an alarm threshold on benign variation, and evaluate detection and false-alarm rates across curated benign and harmful shift pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a benchmark of paired benign and harmful shifts of matched input-space divergence, the structural statistic will rank harmful above benign far more reliably than input-distance detectors, which will alarm equally on both.
why_important: False alarms are why practitioners disable shift monitors, so a signal aligned with harm rather than mere change addresses the operational failure of current monitoring.
why_possibly_novel: Neighborhood-consistency ideas appear in confidence estimation, but as a streaming harm-versus-benign shift discriminator with a matched-divergence benchmark they appear underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Alarm on broken prediction geometry, not on changed pixels.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One benign shift and one harmful shift of similar input divergence, comparing trajectories of the structural statistic against an input-distance detector.
main_risk: Maintaining meaningful neighbor structure in streaming settings with small windows may be too noisy for stable statistics at deployment-realistic batch sizes.
kill_risk: If structural inconsistency fails to distinguish curated harmful from benign shifts, the core discriminative claim is dead.
community_default_belief: Monitoring should watch input statistics, because model-internal signals under shift are untrustworthy by definition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Input statistics cannot encode harm because harm depends on the decision function, and the neighborhood-label structure is precisely where the decision function's health is legible without labels.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the agreement statistic on one benign and one harmful shifted batch from cached features in hours; separation or its absence is immediate.

title: Training shift detectors to predict accuracy impact instead of distributional divergence
one_line_idea: Replace the two-sample-testing objective of shift detection with direct supervised prediction of accuracy impact, trained on a corpus of shifts with measured consequences.
problem: Shift detectors optimize sensitivity to distributional change, but operators need to know expected accuracy impact, and the two quantities diverge badly on benign shifts, causing alarm fatigue and ignored monitoring.
core_hypothesis: Accuracy impact is learnable as a supervised target from batch-level model-internal statistics, using a training corpus of shift events with measured accuracy changes, and such impact predictors transfer across shift types better than divergence statistics repurposed as impact proxies.
core_claim: An impact-trained monitor achieves materially better precision-recall on the operationally relevant event, accuracy degradation beyond a threshold, than any divergence-based detector at matched compute.

falsifiable_prediction: The impact predictor will maintain useful precision on held-out shift families while divergence detectors will show near-chance precision at matched recall because they fire on benign changes.
why_important: Redefining the monitoring target from change to harm aligns the research object with the operational need, potentially reviving deployment of shift monitoring that alarm fatigue killed.
why_possibly_novel: Accuracy estimation under shift exists, but reframing detector training itself around supervised impact prediction with a cross-family transfer evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Detect harm, not difference.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the impact regressor on synthetic corruption events only and test whether it ranks a handful of natural shift events by measured impact better than feature-distance baselines.
main_risk: The corpus of measurable shift events may be too narrow to represent deployment shifts, capping transfer no matter the model.
kill_risk: If impact prediction fails to beat divergence proxies even within the training shift families, the supervised framing offers nothing.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Impact leaves systematic traces in model-internal statistics that a supervised learner can mine, and the missing ingredient has been a labeled corpus of shift events, not a fundamental barrier.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: A small corpus of twenty shift events, a gradient-boosted regressor on batch statistics, and held-out-event ranking checked within a week.

title: Active target labeling strategies optimized for accuracy estimation rather than model improvement
one_line_idea: Design label-acquisition strategies whose objective is the tightest possible estimate of model accuracy on a shifted target population from the fewest labels, as distinct from active learning for model updates.
problem: Organizations audit shifted deployments by labeling random samples, but random sampling is label-inefficient for accuracy estimation, and active-learning heuristics optimize a different objective, model improvement, not estimate precision.
core_hypothesis: Stratifying label acquisition by model confidence and feature-density regions, with allocation optimized for variance reduction of the accuracy estimator, cuts the labels required for a given confidence interval substantially relative to random sampling, especially under shift where errors concentrate.
core_claim: An estimation-optimal labeling policy achieves target confidence-interval widths with a fraction of the labels of random sampling across shifted evaluation settings, and the advantage grows with the concentration of errors in identifiable strata.
method_sketch: Formalize accuracy estimation as stratified survey sampling with model-derived strata, derive allocation rules, and compare interval widths at fixed label budgets against random and active-learning-style acquisition on shifted test sets with known ground truth.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratified estimation-optimal acquisition will reach a given interval width with markedly fewer labels than random sampling on shifted sets, and the empirical savings will track the theoretical variance-reduction predicted from stratum statistics.
why_important: Label-budget audits are the main safety practice for deployed models under shift, and making each audited label count double directly reduces the cost of staying safe.
why_possibly_novel: Survey-sampling theory is classical, but its packaging for shifted-model accuracy auditing with model-internal strata, benchmarked against random audits, appears underexplored in the vision community (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Auditing accuracy is a survey-design problem, not an active-learning problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One shifted test set, confidence-decile strata, optimal allocation versus random sampling at equal budgets, comparing realized interval widths over repeated draws.
main_risk: Stratum statistics estimated from unlabeled data may be inaccurate under severe shift, eroding the allocation's theoretical advantage.
kill_risk: If savings over random sampling are marginal across realistic shift settings, the added protocol complexity is unjustified.
community_default_belief: Random sampling is the correct and essentially unimprovable way to audit accuracy on a new distribution without bias.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unbiasedness does not require uniform sampling, and stratified estimators with model-informed strata are equally unbiased with strictly lower variance when errors cluster, which shift makes likely.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulate audits with confidence-stratified versus random draws on one shifted set with full labels available; variance comparison over resamples takes hours.

title: Three-way drift attribution: splitting observed degradation into covariate, prior, and concept components
one_line_idea: Develop an estimator that decomposes a deployed model's measured performance drop into covariate-shift, label-prior-shift, and concept-shift components using unlabeled target data plus a small labeled slice.
problem: When a deployed model degrades, teams cannot tell whether inputs changed, class frequencies changed, or the input-label relationship itself changed, yet the correct remediation differs completely across these causes.
core_hypothesis: With unlabeled target data and a few hundred labeled target samples, the three components are separately estimable with useful confidence intervals, because each component leaves distinct signatures in importance-weighted performance, prior-corrected performance, and residual disagreement.
core_claim: A staged estimator, importance weighting for the covariate component, confusion-based prior estimation for the prior component, and the labeled-slice residual for concept shift, attributes degradation accurately on constructed cases and informatively on natural ones.
method_sketch: Construct shift scenarios with known component magnitudes by resampling and label-noise injection, run the staged estimator at varying labeled-slice sizes, quantify attribution error and interval coverage, then apply to natural cross-dataset transfers as case studies.
falsifiable_prediction: On constructed scenarios, estimated components will track true injected magnitudes with interval coverage near nominal at a few hundred labels, and attribution error will degrade gracefully, not catastrophically, as components co-occur.
why_important: Remediation is expensive, retraining versus recalibration versus data pipeline fixes, and a validated attribution tool converts guesswork into directed action.
why_possibly_novel: Each component has its own estimation literature, but a unified attribution protocol with coverage guarantees at realistic label budgets appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Give shift a root-cause analysis, not just a detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three constructed single-component scenarios on one dataset, checking that the estimator assigns the bulk of degradation to the correct component in each.
main_risk: Component interactions in natural shifts may violate the staged estimator's separability assumptions, biasing attribution when it matters most.
kill_risk: If single-component scenarios are already misattributed, the decomposition framework fails at its easiest task.
community_default_belief: Distinguishing concept shift from covariate shift is impossible without large labeled target samples, so practitioners should just monitor and retrain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The impossibility intuition ignores how much structure a source model plus unlabeled target data already pin down, leaving a low-dimensional residual that a small labeled slice can identify.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One resampling-constructed covariate-only scenario and the staged estimator, checked in days, tells whether the easiest attribution works.

title: A harm monitor for the adapter: detecting when test-time adaptation is making things worse
one_line_idea: Build a label-free meta-monitor that watches an adapting model's prediction churn and agreement statistics to detect when adaptation itself is degrading performance, triggering rollback.
problem: Test-time adaptation is deployed to fix shift but sometimes causes harm, and no deployed signal distinguishes an adapter that is helping from one that is quietly destroying the model, since ordinary shift monitors watch the data rather than the adaptation.
core_hypothesis: Harmful adaptation produces characteristic signatures, rising churn against the frozen source model on samples the source model was confident about, combined with falling internal diversity, and these signatures separate harmful from helpful adaptation episodes without labels.
core_claim: A churn-based harm score triggers rollback decisions that recover most of the accuracy lost in harmful episodes while rarely interrupting genuinely helpful adaptation, evaluated across streams engineered to induce both outcomes.
method_sketch: Run adaptation across stream conditions known to produce help and harm, log churn stratified by source-model confidence plus prediction-diversity statistics, train a simple harm classifier, and evaluate rollback policies against always-adapt and never-adapt baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Confidence-stratified churn will separate harmful from helpful episodes with high discrimination, and the rollback policy will approach the per-episode oracle choice between adapted and frozen models.
why_important: The main barrier to adopting test-time adaptation in production is the fear of self-inflicted damage, and a validated harm monitor with rollback converts an unbounded risk into a supervised one.
why_possibly_novel: Monitoring literature watches data shift and model accuracy, but monitoring the adaptation process itself as a distinct failure source appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Watch the watcher: the adapter needs its own monitor.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One helpful and one harmful adaptation episode on the same backbone, comparing confidence-stratified churn trajectories between them.
main_risk: Legitimate adaptation under severe shift necessarily changes confident predictions too, so the signature may confuse the strongest genuine adaptations with harm.
kill_risk: If churn statistics fail to separate engineered help from harm episodes, the monitor has no discriminative basis.
community_default_belief: Making adaptation methods intrinsically safe through better objectives is the way forward, rather than adding supervisory layers around unsafe ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No objective has been shown safe across all stream conditions, and defense-in-depth through independent monitoring is the standard engineering answer when component-level guarantees are unavailable.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Log stratified churn during one collapsing adaptation run and one successful run in a day; visible signature differences justify the classifier.
