title: Disentangling optics from chemistry in pathology stain shift with a controlled re-scan protocol
one_line_idea: Design a protocol separating scanner-optics variation from staining-chemistry variation in computational pathology, quantifying each component's contribution to cross-site model degradation.
problem: Cross-site degradation in pathology is attributed to stain variation as a catch-all, conflating staining chemistry with scanner optics, so mitigation research optimizes stain normalization while the optics component remains unmeasured and unaddressed.
core_hypothesis: The two components contribute comparably to cross-site degradation in at least some site pairs, and stain-normalization methods address mainly the chemistry component, leaving a residual optics gap that explains why normalization gains plateau.
core_claim: A factorized evaluation, using slides re-scanned across scanners and serial sections stained at different sites, produces the first componentwise decomposition of the pathology domain gap and reveals which mitigation family each component requires.
method_sketch: Assemble or partner for a factorial dataset where the same tissue is scanned on multiple scanners and serially stained at multiple labs, evaluate fixed models along each factor independently, and measure how existing normalization and augmentation methods reduce each component.
falsifiable_prediction: Model degradation along the scanner factor with chemistry held fixed will be substantial, and stain-normalization methods will reduce the chemistry component much more than the optics component.
why_important: Pathology adaptation research is optimizing against an unfactorized gap, and a decomposition would redirect effort toward whichever component actually blocks clinical deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-scanner and multi-site studies exist, but a deliberately factorial optics-versus-chemistry decomposition with mitigation-family attribution appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Split the stain-shift monolith into its physical causes before optimizing against it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: A small set of slides re-scanned on two scanners, evaluating one fixed model to check whether the optics-only gap is non-negligible.
main_risk: Acquiring factorial tissue data requires clinical partnerships and careful registration, and misregistration between re-scans could masquerade as model degradation.
kill_risk: If the optics-only gap is negligible across scanner pairs, the decomposition confirms the status quo and the mitigation implications evaporate.
community_default_belief: Stain variation, meaning chemistry, is the dominant cause of cross-site pathology model failure, which is why stain normalization is the standard remedy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scanner optics differ in resolution, focus behavior, and color response, all of which are known to move deep features, and their contribution has simply never been isolated from chemistry in evaluations.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one public model on any available same-slide multi-scanner pairs; a measurable accuracy gap in days of work establishes the optics component matters.

title: Site-predictability of features as a pre-deployment predictor of cross-site failure
one_line_idea: Measure how easily a model's features predict acquisition site, and test whether this site-leakage score forecasts the model's accuracy drop when deployed to new sites.
problem: Institutions deploy models to new sites without any predictive measure of how badly they will degrade, discovering failures only after deployment on patient-affecting decisions.
core_hypothesis: Models whose penultimate features admit accurate site classification have entangled site cues into their decision features, and this site-predictability score, measurable before deployment with only multi-site training data, correlates strongly with realized cross-site accuracy drops.
core_claim: A simple leakage probe, a linear site classifier on frozen features, provides a pre-deployment risk score that ranks models by expected cross-site degradation better than in-distribution validation accuracy does.
method_sketch: Across multi-site medical benchmarks, train many models varying architecture and augmentation, fit linear site probes on held-in sites, measure held-out-site accuracy drops, and quantify the probe-drop correlation while controlling for in-distribution accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Site-probe accuracy will predict held-out-site degradation with a strong positive correlation across the model zoo, and interventions reducing probe accuracy, such as site-adversarial training, will reduce degradation roughly in proportion.
why_important: A cheap pre-deployment risk score changes how clinical models are certified, replacing hope with a measurable transfer-risk indicator computed before any new-site data exists.
why_possibly_novel: Site-adversarial training exists as a mitigation, but validating site-predictability as a quantitative pre-deployment predictor of transfer failure across a model zoo appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Audit the features for site fingerprints before the model ever leaves home.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ten models on one multi-site dataset, linear site probes, held-out-site evaluation, and the probe-drop scatter plot.
main_risk: Site predictability may reflect benign nuisance encoding that the classifier head ignores, weakening the correlation the score depends on.
kill_risk: If probe accuracy and cross-site drop are uncorrelated across the zoo, the leakage score is not a risk indicator.
community_default_belief: In-distribution validation accuracy plus data-diversity heuristics are the available basis for judging whether a clinical model will transfer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In-distribution accuracy is silent about which cues the model uses, while transfer failure is caused precisely by cue choice, which the site probe measures directly.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One dataset, three existing checkpoints, site probes and one held-out site, computable in days from cached features.

title: How much of the clinical cross-site gap is calibration rather than discrimination
one_line_idea: Decompose cross-site performance loss of clinical models into discrimination loss and calibration loss, testing whether cheap per-site recalibration recovers a large share of clinical utility.
problem: Cross-site degradation is reported as a single accuracy or area-under-curve drop, conflating genuinely degraded discrimination with miscalibrated thresholds, which have completely different costs and fixes in clinical use.
core_hypothesis: For many site pairs, ranking ability transfers much better than calibrated probabilities, so a large fraction of decision-threshold-dependent utility loss is recoverable by per-site recalibration using a small unlabeled or lightly labeled sample.
core_claim: A decomposition protocol separating discrimination metrics from calibration metrics across site transfers shows the calibration component is frequently dominant at clinically relevant operating points, and simple recalibration recovers most of it.
method_sketch: Across multi-site medical datasets, evaluate transferred models with rank-based and calibration-based metrics separately, compute utility at fixed operating points before and after temperature and prior recalibration with varying calibration-sample sizes, and tabulate the recoverable fraction per pair.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank-based transfer loss will be substantially smaller than operating-point utility loss on most pairs, and recalibration with a small per-site sample will recover the majority of the difference.
why_important: If much of the cross-site problem is calibration, the deployment answer for many settings is a cheap site-onboarding recalibration step rather than expensive adaptation or retraining, changing clinical translation economics.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration under shift is studied, but a systematic discrimination-versus-calibration decomposition of the cross-site gap with recovery curves appears underexplored in the clinical imaging context (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Ask how much of the domain gap is just the threshold being in the wrong place.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One cross-site transfer, comparing rank-metric drop against operating-point utility drop, then applying temperature scaling fitted on a small site sample.
main_risk: Recalibration requires some labeled site data, and in settings where even small labeled samples are unavailable the recovered fraction is theoretical.
kill_risk: If discrimination and calibration degrade proportionally on most pairs, the decomposition offers no actionable wedge.
community_default_belief: Cross-site degradation reflects fundamental representation mismatch requiring adaptation or retraining on site data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ranking is invariant to monotone score distortions while thresholds are not, and site shifts plausibly distort score scales more than score orderings, a distinction aggregate metrics never test.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One public multi-site dataset, one transferred model, rank versus calibrated-utility metrics in an afternoon of evaluation.

title: Harmonization versus adaptation: a matched-budget showdown that scales in the number of sites
one_line_idea: Compare data-side harmonization preprocessing against model-side adaptation for multi-site imaging under matched effort budgets, testing the hypothesis that harmonization stops scaling as site count grows.
problem: Multi-site imaging consortia split between harmonizing data toward a reference and adapting models per site, but comparisons are anecdotal, unmatched in effort, and almost always conducted at two or three sites, hiding scaling behavior.
core_hypothesis: Harmonization quality degrades as the number and diversity of sites grows because pairwise mappings interfere, while model-side adaptation scales more gracefully, producing a crossover in the preferred strategy at moderate site counts.
core_claim: A matched-budget evaluation across increasing site counts identifies a crossover regime and yields an evidence-based decision rule for consortium pipeline design based on site count and heterogeneity.
method_sketch: On multi-site datasets with many sites, implement representative harmonization and adaptation pipelines under equalized tuning budgets, evaluate held-out-site performance as site count grows from two upward, and characterize the crossover against measured inter-site heterogeneity.
falsifiable_prediction: Harmonization will match or beat adaptation at low site counts but fall behind as sites increase, with the crossover point arriving earlier for more heterogeneous site pools.
why_important: Consortia make this infrastructure choice with lasting consequences and no scaling evidence, and a validated decision rule would prevent costly pipeline commitments that fail at scale.
why_possibly_novel: Pairwise comparisons exist, but the site-count scaling axis with matched budgets and a crossover characterization appears unexamined (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The right answer at three sites may be the wrong answer at thirty.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with at least six sites, both pipeline families at two site-count levels, checking whether the performance gap moves with site count.
main_risk: Results may be dominated by the specific harmonization and adaptation implementations chosen, limiting generality of the crossover claim.
kill_risk: If both strategies scale identically, the crossover does not exist and the decision rule reduces to cost preference.
community_default_belief: Harmonization and adaptation are interchangeable tools whose choice is a matter of pipeline convenience and community habit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two strategies have structurally different error-accumulation behavior in the number of site mappings, which convenience-based reasoning never surfaces because small studies cannot expose it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two versus six sites with one method per family on one public consortium dataset; a moving gap within a week of compute indicates the scaling axis is real.

title: Predicting per-site label requirements for fine-tuning from unlabeled divergence measurements
one_line_idea: Fit and validate a curve predicting how many labeled cases a new clinical site must provide for fine-tuning to close its domain gap, using only unlabeled divergence measurements from that site.
problem: Site onboarding negotiations need a label-budget number, but the field can only say label some data and see, making costs unplannable and deterring adoption of otherwise viable models.
core_hypothesis: The labeled-sample requirement to reach a target accuracy at a new site is a stable function of unlabeled divergence measurements between site data and training data, learnable from a corpus of sites with known fine-tuning curves.
core_claim: A divergence-to-label-budget predictor fit on existing multi-site data forecasts new-site label requirements within useful error bounds, converting onboarding from experimentation into estimation.
method_sketch: On multi-site datasets, compute fine-tuning learning curves per held-out site, extract unlabeled divergence features between each site and the training pool, fit a regressor from divergence to curve parameters, and validate prediction error on left-out sites.
falsifiable_prediction: Predicted label budgets will fall within a practically acceptable factor of true requirements for most held-out sites, and prediction error will correlate with how far a site's divergence lies outside the training corpus's divergence range.
why_important: A defensible label-budget estimate is often the deciding input for whether a clinical deployment proceeds at all, making this one of the most decision-relevant quantities the field could learn to predict.
why_possibly_novel: Learning-curve prediction exists for in-distribution scaling, but conditioning cross-site label requirements on unlabeled divergence measurements appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Quote a label price for a new site before labeling anything there.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tuning curves for five sites on one dataset, a two-feature divergence regressor, and leave-one-site-out budget prediction error.
main_risk: Learning curves may depend on site factors invisible to input-level divergence, such as label-quality differences, making budgets systematically underestimated.
kill_risk: If budget prediction error spans an order of magnitude across sites, the estimates are useless for planning and the framing fails.
community_default_belief: Label requirements for a new site are unknowable in advance and must be discovered empirically by incremental labeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Across many observed sites the requirement may vary systematically with measurable divergence, and the unknowability belief may just reflect that nobody has assembled the corpus to check.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate crude divergence measures with fine-tuning label requirements across sites of one public dataset; a visible monotone trend within a week justifies the predictor.

title: Operator identity as a first-class domain variable in ultrasound model transfer
one_line_idea: Quantify how much of ultrasound model performance variance is attributable to the acquiring operator versus the device, and train operator-invariant representations using operator identifiers as environment labels.
problem: Ultrasound model transfer is studied as a device and site problem, but acquisition style, probe pressure, angle habits, and view selection vary per operator, and this human factor is unmeasured as a source of domain shift.
core_hypothesis: Operator identity explains a substantial share of cross-acquisition performance variance, in some settings rivaling device identity, and invariance training over operator-labeled environments improves transfer to unseen operators more than device-invariance training improves transfer to unseen devices.
core_claim: A variance-decomposition study across operators and devices establishes the operator factor's magnitude, and operator-environment invariance becomes a cheap, immediately available training signal since operator identifiers exist in acquisition metadata.
method_sketch: Use ultrasound datasets with operator and device metadata, fit mixed-effects models attributing performance variance to each factor, then train invariance-penalized models over operator environments and evaluate on held-out operators against standard training.
falsifiable_prediction: The operator variance component will be statistically significant and material across tasks, and operator-invariant models will show reduced performance spread across unseen operators relative to baseline training.
why_important: If the human factor is a leading cause of ultrasound domain shift, mitigation strategies change from hardware harmonization to acquisition-style robustness, an entirely different research and procurement agenda.
why_possibly_novel: Inter-operator variability is known clinically, but treating operator identity as a machine-learning environment variable with variance attribution and invariance training appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The scanner is not the domain; the hands holding it are.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one operator-annotated dataset, compare per-operator performance spread of a fixed model against per-device spread to bound the two factors.
main_risk: Operator identity may be confounded with patient population and clinical context, requiring careful adjustment before attributing variance to acquisition style.
kill_risk: If operator variance is negligible after confound adjustment, the human-factor thesis is wrong and device-focused work was correctly prioritized.
community_default_belief: Ultrasound domain shift is primarily a device and manufacturer problem, addressed by multi-device training and image harmonization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Clinical literature documents strong inter-operator variability in acquisition quality, and there is no reason this variability would not propagate into model performance, yet transfer studies have never isolated it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Per-operator accuracy tabulation of one existing model on one metadata-rich dataset, achievable in days, bounds the operator effect immediately.

title: Forward-model re-rendering: physics-based instrument simulation as adaptation for scientific imaging
one_line_idea: Adapt models across scientific instruments by re-rendering source training data through the target instrument's known physical forward model, point-spread function, noise, and spectral response, instead of learning style transfer.
problem: Cross-instrument transfer in microscopy and astronomy is treated with generic learned domain adaptation, ignoring that instrument differences are often precisely characterized physically, information that learned mappings must wastefully rediscover or may get wrong.
core_hypothesis: When the target instrument's forward model is even approximately known, re-simulating source data through it produces training distributions closer to the target in the ways that matter than adversarial or style-based mappings, with none of the hallucination risk of learned generators.
core_claim: Forward-model re-rendering beats learned unpaired translation for cross-instrument model transfer at matched effort, and degrades gracefully with forward-model error, remaining preferable until the physics specification error is large.
method_sketch: Implement parameterized forward models for pairs of imaging instruments, re-render source datasets under target parameters, train on re-rendered data, and compare against unpaired-translation adaptation across tasks, including sensitivity analysis to deliberately corrupted forward-model parameters.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-rendered training will match or exceed learned translation on cross-instrument accuracy in most task pairs, and its advantage will shrink smoothly as synthetic forward-model error is injected, identifying the physics-accuracy threshold where learned methods take over.
why_important: Scientific imaging domains have exact instrument knowledge that mainstream adaptation ignores, and quantifying its value would set a strong, hallucination-free baseline for an entire application family.
why_possibly_novel: Simulation-based augmentation exists per field, but a systematic comparison of physics re-rendering against learned adaptation with a forward-model-error sensitivity analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: When you know the physics of the domain gap, render it instead of learning it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One microscopy pair with documented optics, re-render source data with a point-spread-function and noise model, and compare transfer against one standard unpaired-translation baseline.
main_risk: Real instrument differences may include undocumented components, sample preparation and environmental factors, that the forward model misses but learned mappings capture.
kill_risk: If learned translation beats even well-specified re-rendering, the physics prior adds no value over data-driven mapping and the thesis fails.
community_default_belief: Learned domain mappings are the general solution to instrument shift, with physics simulation seen as brittle and instrument-specific engineering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned mappings hallucinate structure precisely where scientific integrity matters most, while the alleged brittleness of physics models is testable and may be mild for the dominant optical factors.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Blur-and-noise re-rendering matched to one target microscope versus a pretrained translation model on one segmentation task, comparable within a week.

title: Per-site checkpoint selection from unlabeled data instead of one-model-fits-all deployment
one_line_idea: Given a zoo of checkpoints from one training pipeline, select which checkpoint to deploy at each site using only unlabeled site data, testing whether per-site selection beats deploying the single global best.
problem: Organizations deploy the single checkpoint that won central validation to every site, yet different checkpoints plausibly suit different sites, and the information needed to match them, unlabeled site data, is always available and never used.
core_hypothesis: Checkpoint-site affinity is predictable from unlabeled statistics, such as feature-space distance between site data and each checkpoint's training-era statistics, and per-site selection recovers a meaningful share of the gap between global deployment and oracle per-site choice.
core_claim: An unlabeled selection rule applied over a natural checkpoint zoo, seeds, augmentation variants, and training stages, delivers consistent per-site gains over the global-best checkpoint across multi-site benchmarks.
method_sketch: Build a checkpoint zoo from one pipeline, evaluate all checkpoints on all sites of multi-site datasets to establish oracle affinities, test unlabeled selection criteria against oracle and global-best baselines, and characterize when selection helps.
falsifiable_prediction: The oracle per-site spread will be non-trivial, and at least one unlabeled criterion will select checkpoints capturing a majority of that spread, with gains concentrated on sites most divergent from the central validation distribution.
why_important: The intervention requires no new training, only smarter deployment of artifacts organizations already have, making it one of the cheapest possible cross-site improvements to adopt.
why_possibly_novel: Unsupervised model selection is studied for adaptation methods, but per-site routing over an ordinary checkpoint zoo as a deployment policy appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The best model for the average site is the best model for almost no site.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ten checkpoints, four sites, the full oracle affinity matrix, and one unlabeled criterion checked against it.
main_risk: Checkpoint zoos from a single pipeline may be too homogeneous, leaving negligible per-site spread for selection to exploit.
kill_risk: If the oracle spread across sites is within noise, per-site selection has no headroom regardless of criterion quality.
community_default_belief: Deploying the single globally validated model everywhere is both operationally necessary and near-optimal, with per-site differences handled by fine-tuning when they matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Near-optimality is asserted without measuring the oracle per-site spread, and fine-tuning requires labels while selection does not, so the comparison the belief rests on has not actually been run.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an existing checkpoint zoo across the sites of one public multi-site dataset in days; the oracle spread immediately reveals whether the idea has headroom.

title: Gradient-domain bottlenecks for crossing the visible-to-thermal appearance gap
one_line_idea: Route recognition through an intermediate edge-and-gradient representation that preserves geometry while discarding modality-specific appearance, as an inductive-bias alternative to adversarial visible-thermal alignment.
problem: Visible-to-thermal transfer fails because intensity statistics are fundamentally unrelated across the modalities, and adversarial alignment must discover from scratch that geometry transfers while appearance does not, a fact known a priori.
core_hypothesis: An architectural bottleneck computing normalized gradient and edge maps before the main encoder sacrifices little visible-domain accuracy but dramatically narrows the visible-thermal gap, because object geometry survives the bottleneck while modality-specific radiometry is removed by construction.
core_claim: Gradient-bottleneck models transferred zero-shot from visible to thermal imagery outperform adversarially aligned models trained with the same data, and the combination of bottleneck plus light adaptation outperforms either alone.
method_sketch: Implement differentiable normalized-gradient front-ends, train detection and classification models on visible data, evaluate zero-shot and lightly adapted transfer to thermal benchmarks against adversarial alignment baselines, and ablate bottleneck strength against in-domain cost.
falsifiable_prediction: The bottleneck will cut the visible-thermal accuracy gap substantially relative to raw-input models at a modest visible-domain cost, with the largest relative gains on shape-defined categories and the smallest on categories defined by texture or temperature contrast.
why_important: Thermal deployment suffers from scarce labels, so a training-free geometric prior that makes visible-trained models usable at night addresses a real capability gap in surveillance, driving, and search-and-rescue research.
why_possibly_novel: Edge features are classical, but their systematic revival as a modality-bridging bottleneck evaluated against modern adaptation on visible-thermal benchmarks appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Build the modality gap out of the architecture instead of aligning it away.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One detector trained on visible data with and without the gradient front-end, evaluated zero-shot on one thermal benchmark.
main_risk: The bottleneck discards texture cues that carry significant visible-domain accuracy, and the in-domain cost may exceed the transfer benefit for many tasks.
kill_risk: If zero-shot thermal performance does not improve over raw-input transfer, the geometric-survival premise is wrong for these modalities.
community_default_belief: Learned alignment or paired translation is the way to bridge large modality gaps, and hand-designed representations were superseded by end-to-end learning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: End-to-end learning superseded hand design when source and target statistics were related, but across unrelated radiometry the known-invariant structure is exactly what hand design can inject and learning cannot infer without target labels.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train one classifier with a Sobel-based front-end on visible data and test on thermal in two days; the zero-shot delta against the raw baseline settles the premise.

title: Differentiable ISP randomization for camera-pipeline-invariant recognition

core_hypothesis: Randomizing a parameterized differentiable ISP during training covers the space of vendor pipelines far better than image-space augmentation, producing models whose cross-camera degradation is substantially reduced at equal in-domain accuracy.
core_claim: ISP-randomized training beats matched-strength photometric augmentation on cross-camera benchmarks, and the benefit persists even when evaluation cameras use processing styles outside the randomization range, indicating genuine pipeline invariance rather than range coverage.

falsifiable_prediction: Cross-pipeline accuracy drops will shrink markedly under ISP randomization relative to photometric augmentation at matched in-domain accuracy, with the residual gap concentrated in stages the differentiable ISP models least faithfully.
why_important: Camera diversity is among the most ubiquitous and unglamorous causes of deployment shift, and a training recipe that neutralizes pipeline variation would benefit nearly every consumer-imaging application.
why_possibly_novel: Differentiable ISPs exist for image quality optimization, but their use as a randomization axis for cross-camera recognition robustness with held-out-vendor evaluation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Augment in processing-pipeline space, where camera shift actually originates, not in image space where it lands.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One raw dataset, a three-stage differentiable ISP, randomized versus fixed-pipeline training, evaluated across two synthetic vendor-style pipelines.
main_risk: Raw-image training data is scarce, and reconstructing pseudo-raw from processed images may reintroduce the very pipeline biases the method removes.
kill_risk: If pipeline randomization only matches photometric augmentation, the processing-space framing adds engineering cost without robustness benefit.
community_default_belief: Strong photometric augmentation adequately covers camera-to-camera variation, making explicit pipeline modeling unnecessary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Vendor pipelines apply spatially adaptive, content-dependent nonlinear operations that global photometric jitter cannot express, so the augmentation and the true variation live in different function classes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Process one raw validation set through two very different open ISP configurations and measure a photometric-augmented model's accuracy gap in days; a large gap shows augmentation does not cover pipeline variation.

title: Spectral-response-aware band projection before learned adaptation for satellite sensor transfer
one_line_idea: Use the published spectral response functions of satellite sensors to physically project source imagery into the target sensor's band space before applying any learned adaptation, and measure how much adaptation the physics step makes unnecessary.

novelty_hook: Compute the part of the domain gap that has a datasheet, and only learn the part that does not.

title: Explicit ground-sample-distance conditioning for resolution-shift-robust aerial recognition
one_line_idea: Condition aerial recognition models on the known ground sample distance of each image as an input variable, instead of hoping scale augmentation induces resolution invariance.
problem: Aerial models degrade when deployed at ground sample distances unseen in training, and the standard remedy, scale augmentation, forces the model to infer resolution from content even though the true value is available in metadata for essentially every aerial image.
core_hypothesis: Resolution shift is better handled as conditioning than as invariance, because object appearance changes with ground sample distance in systematic ways a conditioned model can exploit, so metadata conditioning outperforms scale augmentation at matched training cost, especially under extrapolation to unseen resolutions.
core_claim: Models receiving ground sample distance as an explicit input generalize across resolution shifts better than scale-augmented unconditioned models, with the largest gains on small-object tasks where apparent size is most informative.
method_sketch: Modify detection and classification architectures to consume the resolution value through feature modulation, train on multi-resolution aerial datasets, and evaluate interpolation and extrapolation to held-out resolutions against scale-augmentation baselines and their combination.
falsifiable_prediction: Conditioned models will beat unconditioned scale-augmented models on held-out resolutions, the advantage will grow with distance from the training resolution range, and ablating the conditioning input at test time will reproduce most of the baseline's degradation.
why_important: Resolution diversity is unavoidable across aerial platforms and altitudes, and exploiting free metadata rather than discarding it is a broadly applicable design correction for the field.
why_possibly_novel: Scale-aware architectures exist for natural images, but explicit physical-resolution conditioning evaluated as a resolution-shift robustness mechanism in aerial imagery appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Stop making the network guess a number that is printed in the image header.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One detector with feature-wise resolution modulation versus its scale-augmented twin, trained on two resolutions and tested on a third.
main_risk: Metadata resolution values may be noisy or inconsistent across datasets, and a model reliant on them could fail when the metadata is wrong.
kill_risk: If conditioning provides no benefit over scale augmentation even under resolution extrapolation, content-inferred scale is sufficient and the conditioning thesis fails.
community_default_belief: Scale augmentation gives models all the resolution robustness they need, making metadata conditioning an unnecessary complication.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation-induced invariance interpolates within the trained scale range but has no mechanism for principled extrapolation, which is exactly where deployment failures occur and where conditioning has a mechanism.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train small conditioned and unconditioned models on two-resolution data and test at a held-out coarser resolution within a week; the extrapolation gap decides the premise.

title: Density-invariance objectives for LiDAR beam-count transfer

falsifiable_prediction: Consistency-trained models will show smaller performance drops on real cross-sensor evaluations than augmentation-only models, and the gap between simulated and real target-sensor performance will be small, validating the resampling fidelity.
why_important: Fleet operators mix LiDAR generations, and label-free portability across channel counts is a recurring, expensive obstacle for both industry-adjacent research and academic benchmark builders.
why_possibly_novel: Downsampling augmentation is common, but a consistency-objective formulation with beam-accurate physical resampling and real cross-sensor validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).

kill_risk: If consistency training adds nothing over augmentation on real cross-sensor tests, the feature-alignment mechanism provides no benefit beyond input exposure.
community_default_belief: Point-cloud downsampling augmentation is the natural and sufficient tool for beam-count robustness in LiDAR perception.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation controls what the model sees but not what its features encode, and density-dependent features can survive augmentation while a consistency objective directly penalizes them.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an augmentation-trained model against its consistency-trained twin on one real sparse-sensor validation set; a few days of training and evaluation decide the increment.

title: Temporal-contrast embeddings as a shared space for event-camera and frame-camera transfer

core_hypothesis: Temporal contrast, brightness change over short windows, is computable from frame sequences and native to event streams, so an embedding trained to be predictive on frame-derived temporal contrast will accept real event data with a far smaller gap than embeddings trained on raw frames.
core_claim: Models trained on frame-video datasets converted to temporal-contrast representations transfer to real event-camera data substantially better than frame-trained models adapted with standard techniques, providing a practical label-transfer path for event vision.

why_important: Event vision is bottlenecked by labels, and a validated transfer path from abundant frame datasets would accelerate the entire subfield while clarifying which event-domain phenomena genuinely require native data.
why_possibly_novel: Event simulation from video exists, but framing the shared temporal-contrast space as a domain-transfer bridge with systematic gap decomposition appears underexplored (novelty not verified).

kill_risk: If converted-data training transfers no better than frame training, the shared-representation premise is wrong for realistic frame rates.
community_default_belief: Event-camera perception requires native event datasets or high-fidelity simulators, since the modality gap from frames is too fundamental for representation-level bridging.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The fundamental-gap view conflates the sensing mechanism with the represented quantity, and the represented quantity, brightness change, is shared and computable from frames at the timescales most recognition tasks need.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One small-scale conversion-and-transfer run on a public event benchmark within a week bounds how much of the gap the shared representation closes.

title: Sensor-physics error-pattern augmentation for depth-sensor transfer
one_line_idea: Model the characteristic error patterns of different depth-sensing technologies, time-of-flight artifacts versus structured-light occlusion shadows, and augment training data with the target technology's error patterns for label-free cross-sensor transfer.
problem: Depth-based models trained on one sensing technology fail on another not because scene geometry differs but because each technology corrupts depth in characteristic ways, edge bleeding, missing regions, and noise structure, that generic augmentation does not reproduce.
core_hypothesis: Depth-sensor domain gaps are dominated by technology-specific error patterns that are well characterized in the sensing literature and simulatable, so error-pattern augmentation matched to the target technology recovers most cross-sensor performance loss without any target training data.
core_claim: Training with physically motivated target-sensor error simulation outperforms both generic depth noise augmentation and learned adaptation with limited target data on cross-technology depth benchmarks.
method_sketch: Implement parameterized simulators of dominant error modes for major depth technologies, apply them as augmentation when training on clean or source-sensor depth data, and evaluate cross-technology transfer on scene understanding tasks against generic-noise and adaptation baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-pattern-matched augmentation will close most of the cross-technology gap, and mismatched augmentation, simulating the wrong technology, will help far less, confirming the mechanism is pattern-specific rather than generic robustness.
why_important: Depth sensors are replaced and mixed constantly in robotics research platforms, and a transfer recipe grounded in documented sensor physics would eliminate a recurring re-labeling cost across the community.
why_possibly_novel: Depth noise simulation exists for graphics realism, but a systematic matched-versus-mismatched error-pattern augmentation study framed as domain transfer appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The domain gap between depth sensors is a catalog of failure modes, and catalogs can be simulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One segmentation model trained with matched error simulation for a held-out sensor technology, compared against generic-noise training on one cross-sensor dataset pair.
main_risk: Error patterns interact with scene content in ways parameterized simulators may capture too coarsely, leaving a residual gap that undermines the headline claim.
kill_risk: If matched and mismatched error simulation help equally, the effect is generic robustness rather than pattern matching, collapsing the physics rationale.
community_default_belief: Depth-sensor differences are minor compared to scene variation, and models robust to scene diversity will handle sensor changes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Missing-data patterns and edge artifacts are structurally unlike scene variation, occupying input regions real scenes never produce, so scene-diversity robustness has no reason to cover them.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure one scene-robust model's accuracy drop on a different-technology depth dataset in days; a large drop confirms sensor error patterns are a first-order problem.

title: Rate-distortion-coverage augmentation for robustness to unseen video codecs

core_hypothesis: The recognition-relevant effect of compression is captured by a low-dimensional position in rate-distortion-artifact space, so training coverage of that space, rather than of codec identities, predicts and produces robustness to unseen codecs.
core_claim: A coverage metric over rate-distortion-artifact space predicts a model's accuracy on unseen codec-setting combinations, and augmentation policies optimized for coverage beat codec-list augmentation at matched budget.
method_sketch: Define artifact-space coordinates from measurable quantities, blockiness, ringing, temporal flicker, and bitrate, map codec-setting combinations into the space, train models with list-based versus coverage-optimized augmentation, and evaluate on held-out codecs including recent standards.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy on held-out codecs will correlate with their artifact-space distance to the training coverage region, and coverage-optimized augmentation will dominate codec lists on codecs far from the list in artifact space.
why_important: Deployed models receive video through transcoding chains their builders never controlled, and a codec-agnostic robustness recipe with a predictive coverage metric addresses this ubiquitous, understudied shift axis.
why_possibly_novel: Compression robustness is studied codec by codec, but the artifact-space coverage formulation with unseen-codec generalization prediction appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Generalize over the physics of compression artifacts, not over a list of software names.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with one codec's ladder, evaluate on a second codec at matched artifact-space positions, and check whether performance tracks artifact-space distance rather than codec identity.
main_risk: New codec generations may introduce artifact types outside any low-dimensional space fit to older codecs, breaking the coverage prediction exactly for the future codecs that motivate the work.
kill_risk: If accuracy on held-out codecs does not track artifact-space distance, the low-dimensional characterization is wrong and coverage optimization has no foundation.
community_default_belief: Compression robustness is obtained by including compressed variants of training data using common codecs, which covers deployment adequately.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Codec lists confound artifact structure with software identity, and deployment transcoding chains routinely produce artifact combinations no list anticipates, as codec settings interact with content.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Cross-codec evaluation at matched bitrates for one model within days establishes whether codec identity or artifact position drives the degradation.

title: Does parameter-efficient fine-tuning really preserve robustness once accuracy is matched

core_hypothesis: Much of the apparent robustness advantage of parameter-efficient methods reflects their position on the same accuracy-robustness trade-off curve rather than a distinct mechanism, and matched-accuracy comparisons will shrink the advantage substantially, though possibly not to zero.
core_claim: A matched-accuracy evaluation protocol across adapter, prompt, and full fine-tuning regimes yields materially different conclusions about robustness preservation than the recipe-matched comparisons the current belief rests on.
method_sketch: Fine-tune a fixed backbone with multiple methods across learning-rate and step grids, select checkpoints at matched in-distribution accuracy levels, evaluate on standard shift suites, and compare robustness at each accuracy level rather than per recipe.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched in-distribution accuracy, the robustness ordering among fine-tuning methods will compress relative to recipe-matched reports, and any residual parameter-efficiency advantage will concentrate at high accuracy-gain regimes rather than being uniform.
why_important: Fine-tuning method choice is now among the most common decisions in applied vision, and the robustness folklore guiding it deserves a controlled test before it hardens into unquestioned practice.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness-versus-fine-tuning studies exist, but a systematic matched-accuracy protocol isolating mechanism from trade-off position across method families appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Compare fine-tuning methods where they stand on the trade-off curve, not where their default recipes happen to land.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one dataset, adapter versus full fine-tuning checkpoint grids, robustness compared at two matched accuracy levels.
main_risk: Matching in-distribution accuracy exactly is fiddly, and residual mismatches could be blamed for whichever result emerges.
kill_risk: If the robustness advantage fully persists at matched accuracy, the artifact hypothesis is refuted and the folklore is confirmed rather than corrected.
community_default_belief: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning inherently preserves pretrained robustness because it changes fewer weights and stays closer to the pretrained solution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Changing fewer weights also typically extracts less in-distribution gain, and the robustness comparison may be measuring that undertraining rather than a preservation mechanism.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two checkpoint grids on one dataset with shift evaluation at one matched accuracy level, achievable within a week on a single backbone.

title: A taxonomy of describable shifts: when does prompting recover vision-language robustness

core_hypothesis: Prompt-describable mitigation works when the shift corresponds to concepts represented in the text encoder's training distribution, such as named imaging styles and sensor types, and fails for statistical shifts lacking linguistic handles, such as specific corruption mixtures or site-specific processing.

falsifiable_prediction: Recovery will be substantial for shifts with common linguistic names and near zero for statistical shifts, with the transition predicted by the familiarity measure, and mismatched descriptors will hurt measurably rather than being neutral.

kill_risk: If recovery is idiosyncratic per dataset with no shift-family structure, no useful map exists and the folklore cannot be systematized.
community_default_belief: Domain descriptors in prompts are a generally useful trick for improving vision-language robustness under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The trick's successes are reported and its silent failures are not, so the folklore may generalize from a biased sample of describable shifts.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One afternoon of zero-shot evaluations with and without sensor descriptors on one named-modality shift and one corruption shift shows whether the describability boundary is real.

title: Retrieval-targeted fine-tuning: adapt on the pretraining-like neighbors of the target domain

why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern embedding spaces make corpus curation a cheap similarity query, so the uncurated-corpus objection describes a pre-retrieval era rather than the current toolbox.

title: Shift-aware distillation: preserving teacher robustness with an unlabeled transfer set from the wild

why_it_might_be_wrong: Function matching on a narrow input distribution constrains the student nowhere else, and shift by definition evaluates the student exactly where the matching never looked.

title: Divergence-profile-scheduled unfreezing as an adaptive alternative to fixed two-phase fine-tuning
one_line_idea: Replace the fixed linear-probe-then-full-tune schedule with per-layer unfreezing ordered and timed by measured layer-wise source-target divergence, so fine-tuning effort concentrates where the shift actually lives.

core_hypothesis: The optimal unfreezing pattern depends on where in depth the domain divergence concentrates, and a schedule that unfreezes high-divergence layers first, keeping low-divergence layers frozen longer, dominates fixed schedules across heterogeneous shift types.
core_claim: Divergence-scheduled unfreezing matches fixed two-phase tuning on shifts it was designed for and beats it on shifts with early-layer divergence, yielding a single adaptive recipe that replaces shift-specific schedule folklore.
method_sketch: Measure per-layer activation divergence between source and target before tuning, derive an unfreezing order and timing from the profile, fine-tune across target tasks spanning sensor, style, and semantic shifts, and compare against linear-probe-then-full-tune and full fine-tuning at matched budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: On early-divergence shifts the profile-scheduled recipe will outperform the fixed schedule which delays early-layer updates longest, while on late-divergence shifts the two will tie, producing the predicted interaction between schedule type and divergence location.
why_important: Fine-tuning schedules are applied millions of times across the field, and replacing a fixed heuristic with a measurement-driven one improves a workflow rather than a single benchmark.
why_possibly_novel: Layer-wise tuning heuristics abound, but deriving the schedule from a pre-tuning divergence measurement with an interaction-based validation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Let a ten-minute measurement design the fine-tuning schedule instead of adopting one recipe for all shifts.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One early-divergence and one late-divergence target task, fixed versus profile-scheduled tuning, testing for the predicted interaction.
main_risk: Divergence profiles may shift during tuning as early updates propagate, making the pre-tuning measurement stale and the derived schedule suboptimal midway.
kill_risk: If fixed schedules match profile-derived ones on early-divergence shifts, schedule adaptivity is unnecessary and the recipe reduces to existing practice.
community_default_belief: Linear probing before full fine-tuning is a robust universal recipe for preserving pretrained features under distribution shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The recipe's supporting evidence concentrates on semantic-style shifts where late layers matter most, and its protection is aimed exactly backwards for sensor-level shifts where early layers carry the divergence.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fine-tune with early-first versus late-first unfreezing on one sensor-shifted target within days; the ordering effect either appears or the premise fails.

title: Frozen-encoder test-time adaptation: stability properties of adapting only lightweight heads
one_line_idea: Restrict test-time adaptation to a lightweight head over a frozen foundation encoder and characterize the stability-versus-peak-accuracy trade against full-network adaptation on long streams.
problem: Test-time adaptation methods designed for end-to-end-trained networks are being applied to foundation-model pipelines, adapting encoder internals whose pretrained structure is the system's most valuable and most fragile asset.
core_hypothesis: For foundation encoders, most recoverable shift error for many shift types lives in the head's mismatch to the target rather than in encoder features, so head-only adaptation captures a large fraction of full-adaptation gains while being structurally immune to the encoder-corruption collapse mode that dominates long-stream failures.
core_claim: Head-only adaptation loses modest peak accuracy relative to full adaptation on short streams but dominates it on long heterogeneous streams, and never falls below the frozen baseline, a safety property full adaptation cannot offer.
method_sketch: Compare head-only, normalization-only, and full-network adaptation over a frozen foundation encoder across short and long streams of varied shift types, tracking peak accuracy, long-run degradation, and worst-window accuracy against the frozen baseline.
falsifiable_prediction: Head-only adaptation will show near-zero long-run degradation and a bounded worst window, while full adaptation will win early windows and lose badly on at least some long streams, with the crossover point measurable and consistent per stream family.
why_important: The field is porting adaptation methods to foundation pipelines without re-deriving their risk profiles, and establishing the safety-accuracy frontier of adaptation scope would guide this transition before bad defaults calcify.
why_possibly_novel: Head-only tuning is common in supervised transfer, but a systematic stability analysis of adaptation scope specifically for streaming test-time adaptation over frozen foundation encoders appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The foundation encoder is infrastructure; adapt around it, not through it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One encoder, head-only versus full adaptation on one short and one long stream, comparing peak and final accuracy.
main_risk: For severe low-level sensor shifts the head may be unable to compensate for encoder-feature degradation, making the safety property irrelevant because peak accuracy is too low.
kill_risk: If head-only adaptation captures little of the full-adaptation gain on most shift types, the trade being characterized is too lopsided to interest practitioners.
community_default_belief: Deeper adaptation is better adaptation, and restricting scope to a head sacrifices most of what test-time adaptation offers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: That belief formed on small end-to-end networks whose features degrade under shift, whereas foundation features are broadly shift-tolerant, moving the recoverable error into the head.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One long-stream run of both scopes over a frozen encoder settles within days whether the stability separation exists.

title: Text-anchored versus image-anchored classifiers under sensor and semantic shift: a two-by-two study
one_line_idea: Test the hypothesis that classifiers built from text embeddings degrade less under sensor shift while classifiers built from image prototypes degrade less under semantic drift, yielding a rule for anchor choice.
problem: With vision-language models, practitioners can define classes by text embeddings or by image-prototype embeddings, but the choice's interaction with the type of expected distribution shift is unstudied, so anchor selection is arbitrary.
core_hypothesis: Text anchors are invariant to imaging-condition changes because they never saw pixels, making them robust to sensor shift but brittle to semantic drift in category appearance, while image prototypes inherit the imaging conditions of their examples, reversing the trade-off, producing a predictable anchor-by-shift interaction.
core_claim: A two-by-two evaluation, anchor type crossed with shift type, reveals a robust interaction that supports a practical decision rule, and mixing anchors adaptively based on estimated shift type beats either pure strategy across mixed conditions.
method_sketch: Construct matched classification tasks under controlled sensor shifts and controlled semantic-drift conditions, evaluate text-anchored, image-anchored, and mixed classifiers per condition, and validate the interaction across model families and datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: The anchor-by-shift interaction term will be significant and directionally consistent across model families, with text anchors winning sensor-shift cells and image anchors winning semantic-drift cells by clear margins.
why_important: Anchor choice is a free design decision made in every zero-shot and few-shot deployment, and a validated interaction rule converts an arbitrary choice into a shift-informed one at no cost.
why_possibly_novel: Zero-shot versus prototype comparisons exist for accuracy, but framing anchor choice as a shift-type-conditional robustness decision with an explicit interaction test appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Where the classifier's anchors came from determines which shifts it inherits.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with a synthetic sensor shift and a temporal semantic-drift split, comparing both anchor types in all four cells.
main_risk: Semantic drift is hard to isolate cleanly in available datasets, and confounded drift conditions may blur the predicted interaction.
kill_risk: If anchor types degrade in parallel across both shift families, the interaction does not exist and anchor choice is robustness-irrelevant.
community_default_belief: Image prototypes, when available, are simply better anchors than text because they occupy the same embedding modality as the queries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same-modality advantage carries the imaging conditions of the prototype set into the classifier, a hidden liability that only materializes under sensor shift, which standard in-condition evaluations never test.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate text versus image-prototype classifiers on one dataset before and after a strong synthetic sensor shift; the differential drop is measurable in an afternoon.

title: Full-trajectory clustering for discovering multiple simultaneous spurious attributes without group labels
one_line_idea: Cluster training samples by the entire shape of their per-sample loss trajectories across training, rather than by final errors, to discover several coexisting spurious-attribute groupings for robust reweighting.
problem: Group-label-free robustness methods identify hidden groups from a reference model's errors at one checkpoint, which collapses all spurious structure into a single error-versus-correct split and misses datasets containing multiple simultaneous spurious attributes.
core_hypothesis: Samples aligned versus misaligned with different spurious attributes are learned at characteristically different times and rates, so full loss-trajectory shapes carry enough information to separate multiple overlapping group structures that final-error splitting cannot distinguish.
core_claim: Trajectory-shape clustering recovers multiple planted spurious groupings on constructed datasets and improves worst-group accuracy over error-split methods on natural datasets with more than one spurious attribute, at no group-label cost.
method_sketch: Record per-sample losses across training epochs, embed trajectory shapes, cluster hierarchically, evaluate recovered clusters against planted multi-attribute structure on semi-synthetic datasets, then plug discovered groups into standard robust-reweighting on natural benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with two planted spurious attributes, trajectory clustering will recover both groupings with high alignment while error-splitting recovers at most a mixture, and downstream worst-group accuracy will order accordingly.
why_important: Real datasets rarely contain exactly one spurious correlation, and methods built on the single-attribute assumption may be leaving most of the achievable robustness unclaimed.
why_possibly_novel: Training dynamics are used for data quality auditing, but multi-attribute group discovery from trajectory shapes feeding group-robust optimization appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: When a sample is learned tells you which shortcut it rode in on.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One semi-synthetic dataset with two planted attributes, trajectory clustering versus error splitting, compared on grouping recovery alone.
main_risk: Trajectory shape may be dominated by example difficulty and label noise, drowning the attribute signal in datasets without strong spurious correlations.
kill_risk: If trajectory clusters align no better with planted attributes than final-error splits, the temporal signal adds nothing and the method reduces to existing work.
community_default_belief: A reference model's final errors adequately identify the samples that break spurious correlations, making error-splitting sufficient for group discovery.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Final errors are a one-bit summary of a rich learning process, and one bit cannot index more than one bifurcation of the data, which multi-attribute datasets require.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Log loss trajectories on one benchmark with known dual attributes and visualize trajectory embeddings in a day; visible multi-cluster structure justifies the pipeline.

title: Cross-environment gradient agreement as a per-feature spuriousness score
one_line_idea: Score each feature dimension by how consistently its gradients point across training environments and prune or down-weight low-agreement features, turning an invariance principle into a direct feature-level measurement.
problem: Invariance-based training methods act on the whole objective and are notoriously unstable to tune, while the underlying idea, that spurious features behave inconsistently across environments, could be applied surgically at feature level but lacks a validated per-feature measurement.
core_hypothesis: The agreement across environments of loss-gradient directions with respect to individual penultimate features separates stable from spurious features, and simple post-hoc down-weighting of low-agreement features improves worst-environment and shifted-domain accuracy without retraining.
core_claim: A per-feature spuriousness score computed from cross-environment gradient statistics identifies planted spurious features on controlled datasets and yields robustness gains via post-hoc reweighting that rival full invariance-training methods at a fraction of their fragility.
method_sketch: Compute per-feature gradient statistics per environment on a trained model, define an agreement score, validate against planted spurious features in semi-synthetic settings, then apply score-based feature reweighting or head retraining and evaluate on subpopulation-shift and domain-shift benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Planted spurious features will receive systematically lower agreement scores than stable features, and post-hoc reweighting by score will recover a substantial share of the worst-group improvement of oracle feature removal.
why_important: A measurement-first approach to invariance replaces brittle end-to-end objectives with an interpretable diagnostic plus a cheap intervention, making robustness tooling accessible to practitioners who cannot afford invariance-training instability.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient agreement across environments appears in optimization-level methods, but its use as a validated per-feature diagnostic driving post-hoc intervention appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Measure spuriousness feature by feature instead of hoping a global penalty finds it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One semi-synthetic dataset with planted spurious dimensions, computing whether the agreement score ranks planted features below stable ones.
main_risk: Feature-level scores may be entangled by rotations of the representation, since spurious information can hide in linear combinations no single coordinate exposes.
kill_risk: If scores fail to separate even axis-aligned planted spurious features, the measurement is unsound and everything downstream collapses.
community_default_belief: Invariance must be enforced during training end to end, because post-hoc analysis of a fitted representation cannot undo reliance on spurious features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reliance lives partly in the head's weighting of features, which post-hoc reweighting can change, and the training-time-only belief may overstate how deeply spurious reliance is baked into features.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Score features of one model trained on a standard spurious-correlation benchmark and compare score distributions for known-aligned versus conflicting groups, computable in hours.

title: Sensitivity audit and small-sample correction for confusion-matrix label-shift estimators
one_line_idea: Quantify how quickly classical confusion-matrix-based label-shift estimators break as their fixed-conditional assumption is violated, and add a correction term estimated from a small labeled target slice.
problem: Label-shift estimators built on source confusion matrices assume class-conditional input distributions are unchanged, but real shifts mix prior change with mild conditional change, and the estimators' failure behavior under such mixtures is undocumented and possibly severe.
core_hypothesis: Estimator error grows sharply and predictably with conditional-shift magnitude, and the leading error component can be estimated and removed using a labeled target slice far smaller than what direct prior estimation from labels would require.
core_claim: A sensitivity study mapping estimator bias against controlled conditional perturbations, plus a hybrid correction combining the confusion-matrix estimate with small-sample labeled evidence, restores accurate prior estimation across realistic mixed-shift regimes.
method_sketch: Construct target sets with controlled prior shift and graded conditional perturbations, map bias surfaces for standard estimators, derive the hybrid correction weighting confusion-based and labeled-slice information by their estimated variances, and validate on natural mixed shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: Standard estimators will show bias growing steeply with conditional perturbation while the hybrid correction stays near-unbiased using only tens to hundreds of labeled target samples, outperforming both pure approaches in the mixed regime.
why_important: Prior-shift correction is a widely deployed lightweight fix whose silent failure under mixed shifts propagates into downstream decisions, and a validated operating envelope plus a cheap repair makes the tool trustworthy.
why_possibly_novel: The estimators and their assumptions are classical, but a systematic bias-surface audit under graded conditional violation with a variance-weighted hybrid repair appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Stress-test the label-shift toolbox where its core assumption bends, and patch it with the fewest labels possible.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset, one estimator, three conditional-perturbation levels, measuring prior-estimation error growth.
main_risk: The bias structure may depend intricately on the classifier and perturbation type, resisting a clean correction term that generalizes across settings.
kill_risk: If standard estimators prove robust to realistic conditional perturbations, the audited failure is negligible and the correction unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Confusion-matrix label-shift estimators are reliable practical tools whose assumption violations cause only minor degradation in realistic settings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The reliability evidence comes from experiments with pure prior shift by construction, and mixed-shift behavior has simply not been mapped, so the belief rests on untested extrapolation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Inject mild image corruption into a prior-shifted test set and measure one estimator's prior-recovery error in an afternoon; sharp degradation validates the audit's premise.

title: Worst-quantile optimization: transporting group-robustness ideas to regression under subpopulation shift
one_line_idea: Develop and evaluate a group-distributionally-robust analogue for regression tasks by optimizing worst-quantile or worst-region error over inferred input-space subpopulations, addressing the classification bias of the robustness literature.
problem: Subpopulation-shift robustness is studied almost exclusively for classification with discrete groups, while regression tasks, depth, pose, and quality estimation, face the same hidden-subpopulation failures with no established robust-training methodology.
core_hypothesis: Hidden subpopulations in regression manifest as regions of input space with systematically elevated error whose contribution to average loss is small, and optimizing a worst-region objective over inferred regions improves those subpopulations at modest average cost, transferring the classification-robustness playbook.
core_claim: A pipeline of unsupervised region inference in feature space followed by worst-region risk optimization yields regression models with substantially better tail-region error under subpopulation shift than average-risk training, across multiple regression task families.
method_sketch: Infer candidate regions via clustering on features or per-sample residual statistics, optimize a smoothed worst-region objective, evaluate on regression datasets with natural or constructed subpopulation shifts, and report worst-region and average error trade-off curves against baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Worst-region error under shifted subpopulation weightings will improve markedly over average-risk training with modest average-error cost, and the improvement will persist when evaluation regions differ from the inferred training regions.
why_important: Regression models underpin measurement-like applications where subpopulation failures mean biased measurements for specific conditions, a harm profile at least as serious as classification group failures yet currently unaddressed by robust training tools.
why_possibly_novel: Distributionally robust optimization theory covers regression abstractly, but a practical inferred-region worst-case pipeline evaluated on vision regression tasks under subpopulation shift appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Bring worst-group thinking to tasks that never had groups in the first place.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One regression task with a constructed hidden subpopulation, comparing average-risk against worst-region training on subpopulation error.
main_risk: Inferred regions may fail to align with the subpopulations that matter at evaluation, making the robustness gains specific to the inference method rather than general.
kill_risk: If worst-region optimization only redistributes error without improving true subpopulation performance under shift, the transfer of the playbook fails.
community_default_belief: Subpopulation robustness is fundamentally a classification-with-groups problem, and regression tasks are adequately served by average-risk training with good features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in the failure mechanism, underrepresented conditions receiving less optimization pressure, is specific to discrete labels, so the classification focus reflects benchmark availability rather than problem structure.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Construct one depth-estimation subpopulation split and measure the tail-region error gap of a standard model in days; a large gap establishes the problem the method addresses.

title: Compositional coverage metrics that predict per-combination transfer failure
one_line_idea: Define a training-set coverage score for attribute-class combinations and test whether it predicts per-combination error under compositional shift better than aggregate distance metrics between domains.
problem: Models fail on attribute-class combinations that were rare or absent in training even when both the attribute and the class were individually well represented, and existing domain-distance metrics aggregate away exactly this combinatorial structure.
core_hypothesis: Per-combination test error is driven primarily by combination-level training coverage rather than by marginal attribute or class coverage, so a coverage score over the attribute-class grid predicts the spatial structure of transfer failure that aggregate divergence metrics cannot see.
core_claim: A combination-coverage metric computed from automatically extracted attributes predicts per-cell error maps under compositional shift with high fidelity, enabling targeted data collection that repairs predicted failure cells before deployment.
method_sketch: Extract attribute labels with pretrained taggers, tabulate combination coverage on training data, measure per-cell test error on compositionally shifted evaluations, quantify the coverage-error relationship, and validate targeted augmentation of low-coverage cells against untargeted augmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-cell error will correlate strongly with combination coverage after controlling for marginal coverages, and topping up the lowest-coverage cells will repair their error at several times the efficiency of uniform data addition.
why_important: Compositional gaps are a predictable, fixable cause of shift failure, and a validated coverage metric turns data collection from guesswork into a targeted repair process.
why_possibly_novel: Compositional generalization is studied in synthetic settings, but a practical coverage-based failure predictor with targeted-collection validation on natural vision data appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The domain gap has a grid structure, and the grid tells you exactly which data to buy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with attribute annotations, per-cell error mapping against combination coverage for one model, before any collection experiments.
main_risk: Automatic attribute extraction introduces noise that may blur the grid enough to weaken cell-level predictions in exactly the rare cells that matter.
kill_risk: If per-cell error is explained by marginal coverages alone, the combinatorial structure is not the failure driver and the metric reduces to standard imbalance measures.
community_default_belief: Transfer failures are characterized by aggregate domain divergence, and per-sample difficulty, not combinatorial coverage, explains within-domain error variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregate divergence can be identical for two domains with opposite combination gaps, so the metric in standard use is provably blind to a failure structure that plausibly dominates practical shifts.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Tabulate per-cell error against combination counts on one attribute-annotated benchmark in a day of evaluation; the partial correlation answers the core question immediately.

title: Prior-corrected abstention: fixing selective prediction under label-prior shift
one_line_idea: Show that abstention thresholds tuned under source class priors systematically misallocate abstentions under target prior shift, and derive a prior-corrected thresholding rule using estimated target priors.
problem: Selective classifiers tune per-class or global abstention thresholds on source data, but when class priors shift at deployment the risk-coverage trade-off silently changes, abstaining too much on newly common classes and too little on newly rare, error-prone ones.
core_hypothesis: The misallocation of abstentions under prior shift is a systematic, computable effect, and re-deriving thresholds using label-shift-estimated target priors restores near-source risk-coverage behavior without any target labels.
core_claim: Prior-corrected thresholding recovers most of the selective-risk degradation caused by prior shift across benchmarks, with the correction magnitude predictable from the estimated prior divergence.
method_sketch: Construct prior-shifted evaluations from standard datasets, quantify realized risk-coverage degradation of source-tuned thresholds, estimate target priors with confusion-based estimators, re-solve the threshold optimization under estimated priors, and compare corrected against uncorrected selective classifiers.
falsifiable_prediction: Uncorrected selective risk will degrade monotonically with prior divergence while the corrected system tracks near-source risk at matched coverage, and correction quality will degrade gracefully with prior-estimation error.
why_important: Selective prediction is the standard fallback for safety-critical classification, and prior shift is the most common mild shift in deployment, so their untreated interaction affects many production systems silently.
why_possibly_novel: Label-shift estimation and selective prediction are each well studied, but their composition into a corrected thresholding rule with degradation analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The abstention threshold encodes the training prior, and nobody updates it when the world's class mix changes.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset, one prior-shifted resampling, realized risk-coverage curves for source-tuned versus oracle-prior-corrected thresholds.
main_risk: Prior estimation error under simultaneous covariate shift may be large enough to make the correction unreliable exactly when shifts are compound.
kill_risk: If source-tuned thresholds show negligible risk-coverage degradation under realistic prior shifts, the problem is too small to warrant the machinery.
community_default_belief: Selective prediction thresholds calibrated on validation data remain valid at deployment, with recalibration needed only under major distribution change.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prior shift is not major distribution change by conventional detection standards, yet it directly rescales the per-class error rates the thresholds were solved against, so validity can fail quietly under changes monitoring ignores.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Resample one test set to double one class's prevalence and plot the realized selective risk of fixed thresholds in an afternoon; visible degradation establishes the problem.
