title: The exchange rate between minority-group labels and majority-group labels under shift
one_line_idea: Quantify how many majority-group training labels one minority-group label is worth for worst-group performance under subpopulation shift, and test whether this exchange rate is predictable from group divergence measurements.
problem: Data collection budgets are allocated without any quantitative model of the relative value of samples from underrepresented subpopulations, even though robustness outcomes are believed to hinge on exactly those samples.
core_hypothesis: The marginal value of minority-group labels for worst-group accuracy exceeds that of majority labels by a large, measurable factor that grows with the feature-space divergence between groups, and the exchange rate is stable enough across tasks to support budget planning.
core_claim: Systematic data-ablation experiments yield exchange-rate curves between group sample counts and worst-group accuracy, and a divergence-based predictor forecasts the exchange rate for new group structures within useful bounds.
method_sketch: On subpopulation benchmarks, sweep group composition grids while holding total budget fixed, fit exchange-rate surfaces from worst-group accuracy outcomes, extract divergence features per group pair, and validate exchange-rate prediction on held-out group structures.
falsifiable_prediction: Exchange rates will be large for high-divergence group pairs and near one for near-identical groups, and predicted rates on held-out structures will fall within a practically useful factor of measured rates.
why_important: Data budgets are the main lever most organizations actually control, and a validated exchange rate converts fairness and robustness goals into concrete, defensible collection plans.
why_possibly_novel: Data valuation and group robustness exist separately, but exchange-rate estimation with divergence-based prediction for budget planning under subpopulation shift appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Put a price tag on underrepresentation, in units of majority samples.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, a coarse group-composition grid at fixed budget, checking whether worst-group accuracy iso-curves imply an exchange rate far from one.
main_risk: Exchange rates may depend strongly on architecture and augmentation, making rates measured in one setup misleading for others.
kill_risk: If iso-accuracy curves imply exchange rates near one everywhere, minority samples carry no special value and the framework is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: More data helps and balanced data is better, but the trade-off is qualitative and budget allocation cannot be made quantitative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The trade-off is an empirical function that ablation grids can simply measure, and its alleged unknowability reflects missing experiments rather than missing structure.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Three composition points on one benchmark, measuring worst-group accuracy movement per swapped sample block, computable within days.

title: Operating curves over a spurious-correlation strength dial instead of single-point benchmarks
one_line_idea: Rebuild spurious-correlation benchmarks with a continuously controllable correlation-strength parameter and report each robustness method's full operating curve, testing whether method rankings depend on the dial position.
problem: Robustness methods are compared at one fixed spurious-correlation strength baked into each benchmark, and conclusions drawn at that single point may not hold at the correlation strengths real datasets exhibit.
core_hypothesis: Method rankings change materially along the correlation-strength axis, with some methods winning only near-deterministic correlation regimes and others dominating mild-correlation regimes, so single-point benchmarks have been selecting methods for an arbitrary operating point.
core_claim: A dial-controlled benchmark suite produces method operating curves that cross, and the crossing structure explains previously puzzling inconsistencies between results on different fixed-strength benchmarks.
method_sketch: Reconstruct standard spurious-correlation datasets with resampling that sets correlation strength continuously, evaluate representative method families across the dial, plot worst-group accuracy operating curves, and test whether cross-benchmark inconsistencies in the literature align with dial-position differences.
falsifiable_prediction: At least some widely compared method pairs will swap rankings along the dial, and the swap positions will be consistent across datasets sharing similar group geometry.
why_important: If rankings are dial-dependent, practitioners need to know their dataset's correlation strength before trusting any benchmark verdict, changing both evaluation practice and method recommendation.
why_possibly_novel: Correlation strength is occasionally varied in ablations, but elevating it to the primary evaluation axis with operating-curve reporting and cross-benchmark reconciliation appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Benchmark verdicts come with a hidden dial setting; publish the whole curve instead.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two methods on one dataset at three dial positions, checking for a ranking swap.
main_risk: Resampling to control correlation strength changes dataset size and composition simultaneously, requiring careful controls to isolate the dial effect.
kill_risk: If operating curves are parallel across all tested methods, single-point evaluation was adequate and the dial adds only cost.
community_default_belief: Benchmark comparisons at the standard correlation strengths generalize to other strengths, since methods that handle strong spurious correlation should also handle weaker ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Methods pay different costs for their robustness mechanisms, and mechanisms that win when correlation is near-perfect can be pure overhead when it is mild, a trade the monotone intuition misses.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One method pair, one dataset, strong versus mild correlation resamplings, rankings compared within days.

title: Is unsupervised validation the real bottleneck: auditing the oracle-selection gap across adaptation methods
one_line_idea: Measure, across many adaptation methods and dataset pairs, how much accuracy is lost by using unsupervised model-selection criteria instead of oracle target-label selection, and compare that loss to the differences between methods.
problem: Adaptation papers report results with tuned checkpoints, but without target labels practitioners must select models with unsupervised criteria, and if selection losses exceed method differences the literature's method rankings are practically irrelevant.
core_hypothesis: For current-generation methods the oracle-selection gap, the accuracy lost by realistic unsupervised selection, is comparable to or larger than typical between-method differences, meaning the field's binding constraint is validation, not adaptation algorithms.
core_claim: A comprehensive audit crossing adaptation methods, dataset pairs, and unsupervised selection criteria quantifies the selection gap distribution and demonstrates whether method rankings survive realistic selection, redirecting attention to criterion research if they do not.
method_sketch: Run a method suite across pairs with dense checkpointing, apply a battery of unsupervised selection criteria per run, record accuracy under each criterion versus oracle, and analyze whether published-style method orderings are preserved under each criterion.
falsifiable_prediction: Selection-induced accuracy losses will rival between-method gaps on a large fraction of pairs, and method rankings under realistic criteria will differ substantially from oracle rankings, with no single criterion dominating across pairs.
why_important: If validation is the bottleneck, the field's marginal effort is misallocated toward new adaptation objectives when criterion research would yield more practical accuracy per unit of work.
why_possibly_novel: Individual criteria have been proposed and compared, but a field-level audit framing the selection gap as the quantity that decides whether method research matters appears underexplored for the current method generation (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Rank the rankings: test whether any published ordering survives label-free model selection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three methods, five pairs, three criteria, comparing the selection-gap distribution against the between-method gap distribution.
main_risk: The audit's conclusions depend on the criterion battery being representative, and a missing strong criterion would overstate the bottleneck.
kill_risk: If realistic selection loses little accuracy and preserves rankings, validation is not the bottleneck and the audit yields a reassuring null.

title: Separating shift difficulty from plain difficulty in held-out-domain benchmarks

core_hypothesis: A substantial fraction of measured domain gaps on standard benchmarks is intrinsic difficulty rather than shift, and this fraction varies enough across domains to distort method comparisons that treat the whole drop as shift-induced.

falsifiable_prediction: Included-domain performance will remain well below other domains' levels for some benchmark domains, revealing large difficulty components, and at least some method comparisons will change sign under the corrected metric.

why_possibly_novel: In-domain versus out-of-domain comparisons exist per paper, but a systematic difficulty-versus-shift decomposition applied as a benchmark audit with ordering-change analysis appears underexplored (novelty not verified).

main_risk: Adding a domain to training changes total data volume and balance, requiring careful matching so the included-domain reference is fair.
kill_risk: If difficulty components are uniformly small, the conflation is harmless and the corrected metric changes nothing.
community_default_belief: The held-out-domain accuracy drop measures distribution shift, which is why it is called the domain gap.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in the held-out protocol separates transferability from difficulty, and domains collected under worse conditions will inflate their gap through a component no generalization method could ever remove.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One with-domain-training run on the benchmark's hardest domain, compared against its held-out score, answers within days how much of that domain's gap was never shift.

why_important: Corruption suites are orders of magnitude cheaper than natural-shift collection, and knowing exactly when the cheap measurement is valid changes how the community evaluates robustness claims.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Corruption suites probe low-level invariances while natural shifts mix semantic and contextual changes, and models can be engineered to excel at the former without any benefit to the latter, especially when training data included corruption-style augmentation.

title: Accuracy-per-FLOP frontiers for test-time adaptation: recosting the leaderboard

core_hypothesis: When methods are placed on an accuracy-versus-adaptation-FLOPs plane, the Pareto frontier is occupied largely by cheap methods at low budgets and the accuracy ordering among affordable methods differs sharply from the headline ordering, revealing that reported progress partly purchases accuracy with unreported compute.

kill_risk: If headline and budgeted rankings coincide across budgets, cost accounting changes nothing and the recosting is redundant.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Costs spanning orders of magnitude cannot be secondary at the edge-compute budgets where adaptation is most needed, and the accuracy-only convention survives because evaluations are run on hardware where nobody feels the cost.

title: Seed-variance accounting for out-of-distribution comparisons: how many published wins are noise

problem: Out-of-distribution scores are hypothesized to vary across random seeds much more than in-distribution scores, yet shift papers routinely report single-seed comparisons with margins that may sit inside the seed-noise band.
core_hypothesis: Seed variance of out-of-distribution accuracy exceeds in-distribution seed variance by a large factor on standard shift benchmarks, growing with shift severity, and a meaningful fraction of margins typical in the literature is statistically indistinguishable from seed noise.
core_claim: A many-seed variance atlas across benchmarks and model classes provides noise bands that contextualize any reported margin, along with a power analysis prescribing the seed counts different margin sizes actually require.
method_sketch: Train many seeds of representative models on standard shift setups, tabulate in-distribution and out-of-distribution variance components, decompose variance sources, checkpoint noise versus data order, and publish per-benchmark noise bands with seed-count recommendations.
falsifiable_prediction: Out-of-distribution seed variance will exceed in-distribution variance severalfold on most benchmarks, and applying the resulting noise bands to a sample of recent margins will place a nontrivial fraction inside them.

novelty_hook: Give every shift benchmark an error bar before anyone claims another win on it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Twenty seeds of one model on one shift benchmark, comparing in-distribution and out-of-distribution variance directly.
main_risk: The atlas may be dismissed as specific to the trained model class, requiring breadth across architectures to earn general authority.
kill_risk: If out-of-distribution variance is comparable to in-distribution variance, single-seed practice is defensible and the atlas is a null contribution.
community_default_belief: Standard single-seed or few-seed evaluation practice, adequate for in-distribution benchmarks, carries over acceptably to shift benchmarks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shifted test sets probe features whose learning is less constrained by the training objective, exactly the components most sensitive to initialization, so the carry-over assumption fails in the direction that flatters noisy wins.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Ten seeds on one small-scale shift setup, variance ratio computed within a week of queue time, immediately indicates whether the concern is real.

title: Do test-time adaptation gains constitute effective robustness or just movement along the trend line

problem: Test-time adaptation methods report raw out-of-distribution accuracy gains, but if those gains merely track the well-documented linear relationship between in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy, the methods provide no robustness beyond what any accuracy improvement would give.
core_hypothesis: A substantial portion of reported adaptation gains lies on or near the trend line fit across unadapted models, meaning many methods effectively relocate models along the line rather than lifting them above it, and the methods that do produce above-line gains share identifiable mechanisms.
core_claim: Trend-line accounting applied to the adaptation literature's method landscape separates true effective-robustness contributions from trend-following ones, reshaping which methods count as progress on robustness rather than on accuracy relocation.
method_sketch: Fit in-distribution versus out-of-distribution accuracy trends over model zoos per benchmark, place adapted models on the plane by evaluating both accuracies after adaptation, measure each method's above-line residual, and analyze which mechanism classes produce positive residuals.
falsifiable_prediction: Method residuals will cluster near zero for a large fraction of tested approaches, with systematically positive residuals concentrated in methods that exploit target-specific statistics rather than generic regularization.
why_important: The distinction determines whether the field is producing robustness technology or repackaged accuracy, and it changes which mechanisms deserve continued investment.
why_possibly_novel: Effective robustness is established for training-time comparisons, but its application as an accounting audit across the test-time adaptation landscape appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Hold adaptation methods to the same trend-line standard that reshaped robust-training claims.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two adaptation methods on one benchmark with an existing published-style trend line, computing above-line residuals for both.
main_risk: Adaptation changes the in-distribution accuracy reference ambiguously, since the adapted model is stream-specific, requiring careful definition of the plane's axes for adapted systems.
kill_risk: If most methods show clearly positive residuals, the skeptical premise fails and the audit becomes a validation of the field's claims.
community_default_belief: Out-of-distribution accuracy gains from test-time adaptation straightforwardly represent robustness improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same raw-gain interpretation was accepted for robust training methods until trend-line accounting showed most gains were accuracy relocation, and there is no reason adaptation methods would be exempt from the same accounting.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Place one popular adaptation method on an existing accuracy-plane plot for one benchmark within days; its residual immediately indicates which story holds.

title: Held-out-shift-family evaluation: measuring method generality across the shift taxonomy

title: Mapping the anti-invariance regime: shifts where spurious features are stable and invariant features move

title: Minimal assumptions for identifying shift decomposition from a source model and unlabeled target data

title: Empirically calibrated proxy bounds: making transfer-risk bounds predictive rather than vacuous

title: Intervention-validity of augmentations under a sensor causal graph: which augmentations are licensed

title: Test-time adaptation as approximate Bayesian filtering over a latent domain variable
one_line_idea: Derive test-time adaptation update rules from first principles as approximate filtering over a latent domain state, obtaining momentum and learning-rate schedules as posterior-update consequences rather than tuned hyperparameters.
problem: Test-time adaptation methods are constructed from heuristics, entropy objectives, momentum choices, reset rules, with no generative account from which their update equations follow, making failures unexplainable and improvements unsystematic.
core_hypothesis: Modeling the stream as observations from a latent, slowly evolving domain state and deriving the approximate posterior update recovers existing adaptation heuristics as special cases, with their hyperparameters determined by interpretable quantities, drift rate and observation noise, that can be estimated online.
core_claim: The filtering derivation reproduces the functional form of popular adaptation rules, predicts their optimal hyperparameters from measurable stream statistics, and its predictions match empirically tuned values across stream regimes, converting tuning into estimation.
method_sketch: Specify the state-space model, derive variational or Kalman-style updates for normalization and adapter parameters, map derived terms onto existing methods, estimate drift and noise online, and compare filter-predicted schedules against grid-searched optima across streams with varied dynamics.
falsifiable_prediction: Grid-searched optimal momenta and learning rates will track the filter-predicted values as stream drift and noise are varied, and mismatches between predicted and tuned values will localize to regimes violating the state-space assumptions, which the theory itself identifies.
why_important: A generative foundation would unify a fragmented heuristic literature, explain when methods fail, and replace per-deployment tuning with online estimation of interpretable quantities.
why_possibly_novel: Bayesian perspectives on adaptation appear informally, but a worked filtering derivation that quantitatively predicts tuned hyperparameters across stream regimes appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: The momentum constant everyone tunes is a posterior update rate the model of the stream should dictate.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Derive the predicted momentum for streams with two known drift rates and compare against grid-searched optima on synthetic streams matching those rates.
main_risk: Real streams may violate the state-space assumptions badly enough that predictions are systematically biased, reducing the theory to qualitative guidance.
kill_risk: If tuned optima do not track predictions even on synthetic streams satisfying the model, the derivation fails its own easiest test.
community_default_belief: Test-time adaptation is an engineering problem where objectives and schedules are justified by benchmark performance rather than derived from generative principles.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same was said of many learning problems before probabilistic formulations organized them, and the stream setting has exactly the sequential structure filtering theory was built for.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One synthetic stream with known drift, one derived prediction, one grid search; agreement or disagreement is established within days.

title: The crossover between investing in robust training and collecting unlabeled target data
one_line_idea: Empirically map the decision boundary between spending resources on robustness-oriented training and spending them on unlabeled target-data collection for adaptation, as a function of shift severity and data-acquisition cost.
problem: Teams facing anticipated shift choose between hardening the model in advance and planning to adapt with collected target data, but the trade-off has never been quantified, so the choice is made by culture rather than evidence.
core_hypothesis: There is a measurable crossover surface, below a shift-severity threshold robust training dominates because adaptation gains are marginal, above it unlabeled collection plus adaptation dominates because no feasible training-time hardening covers severe unanticipated shifts, and the surface's position is estimable from pilot measurements.
core_claim: Matched-resource experiments crossing hardening budgets against collection budgets yield accuracy iso-surfaces whose crossover structure supports a practical decision procedure based on estimated severity and per-sample collection cost.
method_sketch: Define resource-matched arms, augmentation and robust-objective training versus unlabeled collection with source-free adaptation, sweep shift severities on controlled benchmarks, fit outcome surfaces over the budget plane, and extract decision boundaries with sensitivity analysis.
falsifiable_prediction: The dominance ordering between arms will invert as severity increases at fixed budget, and the crossover severity will shift predictably with collection cost, producing a coherent decision surface rather than noise.
why_important: This is the actual resource-allocation question every deployment team faces about shift, and even a rough validated map would replace ideology, robustness-first versus adaptation-first, with measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Robust training and adaptation are compared as methods, but as competing uses of a fixed resource budget with an explicit crossover analysis they appear unstudied (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Turn robustness-versus-adaptation from a philosophical debate into a budget line.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two severities, two matched budget levels per arm, checking whether the dominance ordering inverts.
main_risk: Resource matching across qualitatively different activities, compute for training versus collection effort, requires cost modeling that critics can dispute.
kill_risk: If one arm dominates across all severities and budgets, the crossover does not exist and the decision procedure collapses to a fixed recommendation.
community_default_belief: Robustness should be built in at training time, with adaptation a fallback for cases hardening cannot anticipate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The build-it-in preference reflects when methods papers are written, before deployment, rather than any demonstrated dominance, and severe-shift regimes plausibly favor the adaptive strategy that preference deprioritizes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two-severity two-arm comparison at one budget on a corruption benchmark, achievable within a week, tests whether the inversion exists.

title: Measuring the accuracy floor imposed by domain-class dependence on invariant representations
one_line_idea: Quantify empirically the accuracy cost that removing domain information from representations necessarily imposes when domain and class are statistically dependent, turning a theoretical trade-off into measured curves on real datasets.
problem: Domain-invariant representation learning is applied even when class distributions differ across domains, where theory says removing domain information must also remove class information, but the actual size of this cost on real datasets is unknown, so practitioners cannot judge when invariance is affordable.
core_hypothesis: The accuracy floor from enforcing domain invariance grows measurably with the estimated mutual information between domain and class variables, and on many real multi-domain datasets this dependence is strong enough that full invariance costs several points of accuracy, explaining observed underperformance of aggressive alignment.
core_claim: A measurement pipeline combining dependence estimation with invariance-strength sweeps produces floor curves per dataset that quantitatively predict where on the invariance spectrum optimal performance sits, replacing the invariance-is-free assumption with a measurable budget.
method_sketch: Estimate domain-class dependence on multi-domain datasets, train models along an invariance-strength continuum measured by domain-probe accuracy on features, record task accuracy per invariance level, and test whether the accuracy-optimal invariance level correlates with estimated dependence across datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: Datasets with high domain-class dependence will show accuracy peaking at partial invariance and declining toward full invariance, while near-independent datasets will tolerate full invariance without cost, with the peak position tracking the dependence estimate.
why_important: The result would give the field a quantitative rule for how much invariance to buy per dataset, preventing both wasteful over-alignment and superstitious avoidance of alignment.
why_possibly_novel: The information-theoretic trade-off is known abstractly, but systematic empirical floor curves with dependence-based prediction of the optimal invariance level appear unmeasured (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Price the invariance the objective is demanding before paying for it.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One high-dependence and one low-dependence dataset, five invariance strengths each, checking whether accuracy-versus-invariance curves differ as predicted.
main_risk: Controlling invariance strength precisely is difficult, and probe-based measurement of achieved invariance may itself be unreliable at high strengths.
kill_risk: If accuracy is flat across invariance levels regardless of measured dependence, the theoretical floor is empirically negligible and the budget framing is unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Domain-invariant features are the goal of adaptation, and more invariance is better so long as training remains stable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The goal statement predates careful attention to label-distribution differences across domains, and in their presence the mathematics says the goal destroys class information, a cost the community treats as an edge case but may be the common case.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Sweep alignment weight over one label-skewed adaptation pair and plot accuracy against probe-measured invariance in days; a visible interior optimum substantiates the floor.

title: Equivariance versus augmentation under group-structured domain shift: a controlled comparison
one_line_idea: Test whether architectures equivariant to a known nuisance group outperform augmentation over the same group specifically when domain shift moves along that group, and lose their advantage otherwise, mapping when structure beats data.
problem: When the nuisance structure of an anticipated shift is known, rotations for aerial imagery or spectral scalings for multispectral sensors, practitioners can encode it architecturally or cover it by augmentation, and the field lacks a controlled account of when each investment wins under actual shift.
core_hypothesis: Equivariant architectures generalize to group elements beyond the training range where augmentation-trained models degrade, so equivariance wins precisely under group-structured extrapolative shift, while under shifts unrelated to the group the architectural constraint is neutral or slightly costly.
core_claim: A controlled comparison crossing model type with shift type, within-group interpolation, within-group extrapolation, and off-group shifts, establishes a decision rule for when to pay the architectural cost, supported by consistent effects across two group structures.
method_sketch: Implement equivariant and standard architectures with matched capacity for rotation and spectral-scaling groups, train with matched augmentation budgets, evaluate under group-interpolation, group-extrapolation, and unrelated shifts, and compare degradation profiles across the design.
falsifiable_prediction: Equivariant models will show flat degradation across group-extrapolative shifts where augmented standard models fall off sharply beyond their training coverage, while both will degrade similarly under off-group shifts, yielding the predicted interaction.
why_important: Architecture choices are long-lived commitments, and a validated rule for when group structure pays off under shift converts equivariance from an aesthetic preference into a costed engineering decision.
why_possibly_novel: Equivariance-versus-augmentation comparisons exist for in-distribution efficiency, but framing the comparison around domain-shift extrapolation with off-group control conditions appears underexplored (novelty not verified).
novelty_hook: Structure beats data exactly where the shift walks along the group, and nowhere else.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One rotation-group setup, equivariant versus augmented models, evaluated on held-out rotation ranges and one unrelated corruption shift.
main_risk: Capacity matching between equivariant and standard architectures is subtle, and mismatches could masquerade as structure effects.
kill_risk: If augmented models match equivariant ones even under far group extrapolation, augmentation coverage suffices and the architectural investment has no shift-robustness case.
community_default_belief: Sufficient augmentation over a known nuisance group makes architectural equivariance unnecessary, since the model learns the invariance from data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned invariance is interpolative within the augmented range, and deployment shifts that extend the group range, new sensor orientations or spectral gains, probe exactly the extrapolative regime where learned and structural invariance should part ways.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train both model types on a restricted rotation range and evaluate at held-out rotations within a week; the extrapolation gap either appears or the structural case collapses.
